title: Trump Is an Easy Mark for Putin
excerpt: Late last night, President Trump announced a “massive” deal to buy diesel fuel from Russia
body: Late last night, President Trump announced a “massive” deal to buy diesel fuel from Russia
For the American truckers and farmers Trump claims to be serving, the deal means little or nothing
Trump may not know or may not care that his latest gambit will not reduce diesel prices
His poll numbers are plunging to Herbert Hoover levels
He needs a last-minute electioneering gimmick
But while the deal will not benefit American consumers, it has immense consequences for others
For Vladimir Putin’s Russia, the deal is a potential lifesaver
For war-ravaged Ukraine, it is the most outrageous and heartless Trump betrayal to date
For Trump’s entourage, the deal promises corruption opportunities on a multibillion-dollar scale

And for people trying to understand the Trump presidency, the deal is further proof of the accusation that Nancy Pelosi flung in Trump’s face in 2019: “With you, all roads lead to Putin.” The United States is a diesel superpower
It is one of the world’s largest producers and exporters of diesel fuel
U.S. refineries produce about 5.2 million barrels of diesel a day
Americans consume about 3.7 million barrels a day
The surplus is sold abroad: In recent months exports have run above 1.5 million barrels a day

The United States imports some diesel fuel from Canada, about 154,000 barrels a day, owing to the peculiarities of pipeline and shipping networks: It’s cheaper to supply New England from the Canadian refinery in New Brunswick than from U.S. refineries along the Gulf Coast
By comparison, Trump’s Russia deal is for 2.25 million barrels : the equivalent of about 16 hours’ worth of U.S. consumption, 10 hours’ worth of U.S. production, or 14 days’ worth of Canadian imports
Unfortunately for U.S. diesel consumers, the price of diesel fuel is set by global markets, not North American ones
Trump’s Iran war has disrupted fuel supplies from the Middle East, including diesel supplies
Before the war, Europe imported more than half a million barrels of diesel a day from the Persian Gulf
The world’s second-biggest diesel exporter used to be Russia, which shipped about 817,000 barrels a day in 2025

When the Iran war raised energy prices, Russia was positioned to profit. [ David Frum: Why Trump didn’t predict the gas-price spike ] The United States in the past tried to help Ukraine by sanctioning Russian energy exports
Trump sometimes pretended to support this policy
In September 2025, for example, Trump proclaimed a tariff on India, ostensibly to punish India for buying Russian oil—but then lifted it in February
So the Ukrainians took matters into their own hands
As Russia has intensified its horrific drone and missile attacks on Ukrainian civilians, Ukraine has struck back with a devastating campaign against Russian energy infrastructure, including diesel
By late summer 2026, the Ukrainians estimated that they had shut down 43 percent of Russian refinery capacity
According to Ukrainian reports, Russian production of oil of all kinds plunged from 5.6 million barrels a day before the Iran war to 4.1 million barrels by late summer 2026
Russia imposed a ban on diesel exports in July
Friends of Ukraine hailed the attacks on Russian energy infrastructure as a war-changing success
Trump saw a threat to Republican hopes in the midterms
Curbs on Russian fuel exports helped push the price of diesel fuel in the U.S. above $5 a gallon in July, then higher than $6 a gallon in September
Since Trump’s return to power in 2025, the Putin regime has dangled lucrative deals in front of the president’s entourage

The Wall Street Journal reported in November 2025 about secret conversations in Miami the previous month between the head of Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, Kirill Dmitriev, and Trump’s negotiators, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: “For the Kremlin, the Miami talks were the culmination of a strategy, hatched before Trump’s inauguration, to bypass the traditional U.S. national security apparatus and convince the administration to view Russia not as a military threat but as a land of bountiful opportunity, according to Western security officials

By dangling multibillion-dollar rare-earth and energy deals, Moscow could reshape the economic map of Europe—while driving a wedge between America and its traditional allies.” The report noted that Dmitriev “found receptive partners in Witkoff—Trump’s longtime golfing partner—and Kushner, whose investment fund, Affinity Partners, drew billion-dollar investments from the Arab monarchies whose conflict with Israel he had helped mediate.” The New York Times reported last week about an even more brazen Russian offering: a multibillion-dollar oil deal for assets owned by Russia’s Lukoil, which would directly benefit a Trump donor and two Middle Eastern groups that have done business with Kushner or Witkoff’s family. (A spokesman for Steve Witkoff said of the Times story that Witkoff “has no conflict of interest and no financial stake in this matter.” Of the Wall Street Journal story, a source described as “familiar with Witkoff’s thinking” said “the envoy is confident that any settlement with Russia would benefit America broadly, not just a handful of investors.”) But all these apparently enticing Russian schemes come with a catch: Russian energy assets are not worth much if those assets are regularly wrecked by Ukrainian drones
This makes plain the implicit quid pro quo in these lucrative deals offered to Trump’s family and friends: If you compel Ukraine to surrender, we will enrich you beyond reckoning
Putin is attempting to leverage Russia’s most strategic asset in his war on Ukraine: Trump’s weakness for corruption
The 2.25 million barrels of diesel Putin offered Trump will have zero net impact on world energy markets or the world price of diesel
But accepting those barrels will collapse the U.S.-led sanctions regime on Russia—and align Trump with Putin against the Ukrainian air attacks on Russian energy production
Trump stopped providing aid to Ukraine long ago
But the U.S. still provides Ukraine with crucial intelligence information

title: Those Books of Smut and Wonder
excerpt: Do your heroes weep? Do they swoon with lust? Are they really confused by their new magical powers? Then you’re already a fan of romantasy
body: Do your heroes weep? Do they swoon with lust? Are they really confused by their new magical powers? Then you’re already a fan of romantasy
For those still waiting to discover romantasy: It’s fantasy, with strong female protagonists and fewer boring bits—the long treks over major landforms in hard weather
Sex is plentiful, but sex is not the genre’s defining feature
You can go chapters before encountering a reference to someone’s toned body

Far more significant are feelings and friendships between the heroes: enchanted beings with relatable self-esteem issues who don’t just seek and fight but also yearn and banter as they face down enemies who aren’t only evil, but super bitchy too
Then the heroes cry and have orgasms (sometimes they orgasm first and cry after)
In the kingdom of romantasy, one writer reigns supreme: Sarah J
It sounds like a missile-defense system or an autoimmune condition, but it’s the acronym for one of the most popular series of novels for adults written in the 21st century
A Court of Thorns and Roses is the first of many books about Feyre Archeron, a young huntress spirited into the faerie realm
Humans hate the leaders of the faerie world, called the High Fae, who once enslaved them
But as soon as one bursts through Feyre’s door, having shape-shifted into the body of a green-eyed, bearlike beast, the reader thinks, I bet some of these guys are going to be hot
Feyre falls in love and breaks a curse and brings down a depraved fae queen, and that’s just in the first book—eventually she’ll assemble a crew of beloved sidekicks and a heap of supernatural powers
On any given week, you can see every book in the series stacked in a column on the New York Times best-seller list
If you combine ACOTAR with Maas’s two other series, Throne of Glass and Crescent City , she has sold some 75 million copies
The Lord of the Rings has likely sold more than twice that, but J
After A Court of Thorns and Roses come courts of: Mist and Fury , Wings and Ruin , Frost and Starlight , and Silver Flames
Fans waited five long years for the sixth book

Would the next court have one syllable and two syllables? Would the decent faeries stop the awful ones from slaughtering and re-enslaving the humans? Then Maas announced, in a rare interview on the podcast Call Her Daddy , that she would actually be releasing three new books—one in October, one in January, and one more after that—and people lost their minds
Right away a question shot into the inboxes of America’s bookstores: Are you having a midnight release party? Tickets sold out
For one “fantasy ball” at a bookstore in El Paso, Texas, they sold out in 12 hours
A second party was announced; it sold out too

Book clubs began rereading all of the courts in preparation. [ Read: The publishing industry’s most swoon-worthy genre ] On social media, bets were made about which of Feyre’s sisters or friends the new books would focus on, and what color the covers would be (Maas hadn’t done purple yet)
In August, images of the next two jackets—­for A Court of Splintered Harmony and A Court of Forgotten Melody — lit up Times Square

They were ombré! But search The New York Review of Books or the London Review of Books for Maas, and you’ll find references to a German foreign minister, a river, the Pynchon character Oedipa Maas —and no trace of Sarah J

The New Yorker ’s culture podcast summed up the low end of romantasy as “customer service wrapped in self-care wrapped in literature,” though one of the critics admitted that she’d loved A Court of Thorns and Roses

Hear enough writers lament that the only books that sell now are faerie or dragon or elfpunk porn, and you start to get the feeling that the literary establishment is committed to resenting this rare bright spot in the publishing industry
Maas, now 40, was a teenager when she wrote an epic fairy tale about a young assassin who can slit throats as well as waltz at balls for a fiction site
That story was published by Bloomsbury, in 2012, as Throne of Glass
The novels that followed took off on #BookTok and then in real life thanks to a generation of former Harry Potter fans who now had jobs, babies, and stymied sex drives
These people (women) started reading (or listening)

Fewer Americans are reading for pleasure every year, and yet people keep opening bookstores—romance bookstores in particular ( more than 100 in the past year and a half alone , according to the American Booksellers Association)
Zella Funk­houser, a high-school science teacher, runs three book clubs at the newly opened Bonfire Bookstore & Yarnery, in Shenandoah County, Virginia

She told me that she picked up A Court of Thorns and Roses in 2023, after having gone “years without really reading a whole lot.” Then back-to-back snowstorms hit, and her husband, who does road work for the state, spent days out plowing

Alone at home behind a wall of snow, Funkhouser devoured all five books. “We didn’t have internet; we didn’t have power,” she told me. “I was obsessed.” On a Saturday night in June, her book club discussed Thorns and Roses
Erin was reading the series for the third time, Tiffani for the fourth, Abby for the fifth. “We’re not reading high literature, let’s be honest,” one of the women acknowledged
But they weren’t looking for formal innovation; they were looking to be inspired and turned on
It’s true that you’re rarely transported by ACOTAR ’s language

Characters say things like “I admire your balls, Feyre.” Sometimes they make me laugh. “Shall we assist you, or just flap here, talking?” a leader of winged reinforcements asks, when it seems the battle has been lost
Characteristic of the genre, the books remix familiar stories
The first meal in Beauty and the Beast , minus the dancing silverware

title: Even Good Friends Can Be Bad Texters
excerpt: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight
body: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight
Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning. “Forgive the bad texters,” Julie Beck wrote in a recent Atlantic essay
Beck is one of them: She routinely leaves messages unanswered for days or even weeks, not because she doesn’t care but because she gets distracted, is burned-out, or simply forgets
Yet in a world where everyone is expected to be constantly reachable, a delayed reply can easily be mistaken for indifference
Texting has made staying in touch easier than ever, but it has also turned communication into a near-constant obligation
A third of Americans report feeling overwhelmed by the number of texts they need to respond to, Beck writes
People have felt guilty about unanswered correspondence for centuries, but technology has escalated both those expectations and the anxiety that comes with meeting them
Being a good texter, Beck suggests, isn’t the same as being a good friend
Someone who takes days to reply might still be the first to show up when you need them
So the next time a friend leaves you on read, consider giving them the benefit of the doubt
And if you’re the one with a growing pile of unanswered messages, maybe give yourself a little grace too

title: Megyn Kelly’s Extreme Makeover
excerpt: Do you remember Megyn Kelly? I once walked past her in a Chicago O’Hare bathroom in 2016, shortly after Donald Trump had won his first presidential election, an
body: Do you remember Megyn Kelly? I once walked past her in a Chicago O’Hare bathroom in 2016, shortly after Donald Trump had won his first presidential election, and was momentarily stopped in my tracks by both her nuclear-grade charisma and her pixie cut
For a woman to have short hair on Fox News, where Kelly was a star anchor at the time, seemed as seditious to the network’s established order as reading Judith Butler or Karl Marx live on air

But this was a moment during which Kelly seemed to be leaning into the role of crusader for women—speaking out about being sexually harassed by the former Fox News CEO Roger Ailes and so inflaming Trump with her rigorous questioning during one debate that he later insinuated on CNN that she must have had her period

All of which makes it so disconcerting, 10 years later, to see Kelly now, on her daily SiriusXM and YouTube show, cursing and sneering with long barrel curls and the gusto of someone hosting not a discussion of polling data but a Two Minutes Hate. “I’m just gonna be honest, she’s not the most attractive gal,” Kelly said on Monday, discussing the anonymous woman who has filed a lawsuit detailing her alleged gang rape at Cornell University. (The men named in the lawsuit have denied any wrongdoing.) “She’s extremely”—here Kelly screwed up her face in disgust—“ beefy in, like, her arms and her legs
She has a whole video online talking about her cankles
Admired, wanted—some women even foolishly say loved —by these guys at Cornell

She’s probably thrilled to be so admired because she clearly didn’t grow up the incredibly beautiful one.” [ Sophie Gilbert: Is college getting less safe for women? ] We’ve seen some drastic heel turns in the media over the past few decades, but none quite as morally appalling as a former self-described advocate for female empowerment suggesting that a woman in this situation might have craved the attention because no one would have wanted to have sex with her otherwise. (Not to mention the contentions that the woman Kelly seems to be referring to, whose name has been leaked by some commentators, is not actually Jane Doe, based on her age and the fact that she would have been too young at the time to attend college.) Normally, I have a pretty strong constitution for this kind of bad-faith rage bait
But Kelly’s display this week of what I can describe only as performative hysteria has been hard to watch
Less than a minute into her show on Monday, she invoked the Salem witch trials
Twenty-three minutes in came her first pronounced use of the word fuck (I counted seven in total)
That the whole performance was interspersed with ad reads for supplements and a tiny avatar of Kelly pointing giddily at the “Subscribe” button just added to the cognitive dissonance
It felt like watching morning television in Gilead
I’ve been stuck all week on the question of how much of Kelly’s performance these days is attention-seeking behavior for the YouTube algorithm and how much is reflective of what she actually believes
Kelly, 55, grew up outside of Albany, where she also went to law school, becoming an editor at the Albany Law Review
She was an attorney for almost a decade, but has said that watching live newscasts on 9/11 inspired her to change careers and become a TV reporter
She was hired full-time at Fox News in 2004
Before long—according to her allegations—Ailes began making inappropriate comments, such as how sexy he imagined her bras must be

In January 2006, Kelly claimed, Ailes tried to kiss her; after his third attempt, she said she got up and walked out of his office. (Ailes denied Kelly’s allegations; he died in 2017.) Three months later, Kelly made a name for herself with her skeptical coverage of the Duke lacrosse team’s alleged gang rape of an erotic dancer. (The woman in question eventually admitted to fabricating the assault.) All of this matters, I think, because it communicates to what extent Kelly’s apparent worldview—where she herself can face sexual harassment due to patriarchal power structures that protect and even reward abusive men, but other women are likely lying—has been shaped by her rise and fall on TV news

In 2016, she declined in an interview with NPR to call herself a feminist. (She dislikes the label, she said, as though it’s just a branding issue.) Her 2016 book, Settle for More , was published just a week after Trump won the presidential election, and became a No. 1 New York Times best seller

Reviews were lukewarm, perhaps because of the news environment: “For all the disgust that she claims to feel for the misogyny and male entitlement” that seemed to be ramping back up in the national culture, Isaac Chotiner wrote in Slate , “and for all the personal harm it caused her, our bleak future is one in which Megyn Kelly is likely to find herself right at home.” But things took a downward turn when Kelly left the Fox fold

In 2017 she was poached by NBC News, which offered her an annual salary reported to be more than $20 million to host a daytime talk show, Megyn Kelly Today , and a Sunday-night news magazine, which was criticized for softball interviews with Vladimir Putin and Alex Jones and ultimately canceled
Megyn Kelly Today didn’t fare much better—Kelly, with her flinty self-possession, was criticized for being too chilly for daytime TV

During her first week, she awkwardly grilled Jane Fonda about whether she’d had plastic surgery while Fonda was promoting a movie next to her co-star Robert Redford. (“We really want to talk about that?” Fonda responded, after an agonizing few seconds of icy silence.) In October 2018, Megyn Kelly Today was canceled when Kelly defended blackface in a segment on Halloween costumes
A few months later, her NBC contract expired
This moment seems to have influenced Kelly’s current persona

Public humiliation is hard for anyone to endure, but for someone with a renegade streak (“I’ve never been a ‘pc’ kind of person,” she reportedly wrote in her apology email to NBC staffers after her blackface comments), seeing so many people celebrating her failure must have been immensely painful

By the time The Megyn Kelly Show launched as a podcast in September 2020, mid-pandemic, Kelly was snidely describing her guests as lefties, complaining about the assault allegations against the Supreme Court justice Brett Kavanaugh, and raging at the “dishonesty” of the press covering Trump
The pivot, whatever its reason, seems to have done what it was supposed to
Kelly has more than 4 million YouTube subscribers and The Megyn Kelly Show is one of the top podcasts in the country

Because Kelly is half-Italian and half-Irish, she told Semafor in 2024, “if you choose to watch the show, you will definitely glean something from the hand gestures and facial expressions that you might not pick up from listening alone.” Having watched Kelly all week, I can attest to this

Although she injects real poison in her voice to rage against, say, the singer Olivia Rodrigo for expressing support for Cornell’s Jane Doe, she accompanies this with the shrugs and waves of a waiter trying to describe tonight’s special of veal parmigiana. “Olivia, in sum, you don’t know what the fuck you’re talking about,” she said. “Shut up and stick to singing
I liked you better when you were in front of a microphone singing your weird little depressing songs
You don’t know what you’re talking about.” You can sense she’s imagining clips being spliced for TikTok and Instagram, and tailoring her delivery to provoke maximum indignation

As a rant, it feels much too phony—and cynical, given how fury seems to be the sole emotion that can build an audience in 2026, and the fact that Rodrigo is one of the most popular women alive. (“The only reliable way to reach mainstream or even moderate recognition against all the noise,” Rebecca Jennings wrote earlier this year in New York magazine, “is to either carpet-bomb social media with clips or to enrage wide swaths of the public.”) But in moments, Kelly does seem to slip out of character
Although she seems perfectly happy excoriating Jane Doe, Kelly draws the line at revealing her name. “I know her name,” she said on Monday. “It’s been well publicized online
But no one in the mainstream media has said it
And as you know I’m seriously considering just saying it
And the reason I haven’t is because I don’t want to do anything to hurt this young woman, to get her hurt, or to add to the pain I’m sure she’s feeling.” Her voice is surprisingly gentle

Could it be that this woman who herself had to hire armed guards for her family after being personally targeted by Trump actually feels for someone caught in a similar nightmare? Is all this spewed-out ire and provocation really just about a reward as soul-rotting as clicks and followers? I don’t think Megyn Kelly will ever tell us, but I have my suspicions.

title: The Best Protein Source Is Hiding in Plain Sight
excerpt: Somehow, America has yet to reach peak protein
body: Somehow, America has yet to reach peak protein

Even after David bars have gone viral for being bricks of essentially pure protein and Starbucks has rolled out lattes topped with “protein cold foam,” new and somehow weirder protein-laced products keep hitting shelves

You can now buy protein Honey Nut Cheerios, protein popcorn and PopCorners, protein sodas, protein ranch dressing, and protein chips. (Doritos launched a nacho-cheese-flavored version with 10 grams of protein per one-ounce serving.) In an era of GLP-1 drugs and peptide stacks and Oura rings and self-optimization, of wellness influencers and looks-maxxers, everybody seems to be doing everything they can to eat as much protein as possible
The magical macronutrient will supposedly make you more muscular, or more toned, or thinner—or something, really anything, just better
Amid the protein frenzy, regular food seemingly doesn’t cut it anymore

Why order a simple flat white when you can instead sip a Dunkin’ Nutty Pumpkin Iced Protein Latte? [ Read: America has entered late-stage protein ] Into the fray, I would suggest a humble alternative: Have some yogurt
Calorie for calorie, Greek yogurt has more protein than Chipotle’s High Protein Low Calorie Bowl, Kraft’s new PowerMac, or yes, a Dunkin’ Nutty Pumpkin Iced Protein Latte
So do some traditional yogurts, as well as other fermented options in the dairy aisle such as skyr and kefir
And that’s if you opt for the full-fat, luscious kind (which I recommend)
Nonfat Greek yogurt, which is lower in calories, is roughly as protein-dense as a David bar—with the added benefits of having just two ingredients (milk, culture) and not tasting like plastic
Yogurt is not only full of protein but also good for your bones, your digestion, and your immune system
Yogurt is an ingredient: Eat it plain or bake with it, use it as the base of a sauce or dip, throw it in a marinade or soup
Sure, some yogurts have added sugars , but so does a Starbucks Iced Banana Protein Cream Matcha
And as far as health fads go, yogurt is typically probiotic

All things considered, yogurt may be the easiest protein of all. [ Read: Let’s not fool ourselves about yogurt ] In spite of everything it has going for it, yogurt has not been the face of the protein craze
Perhaps that’s because yogurt is not splashy or technologically innovative or referred to by a trademarked proper noun
A David bar may taste different and have distinct packaging from an RxBar or a Jacob protein bar made with beef tallow, but all plain yogurt is the same

Though some companies have released “protein-enhanced” yogurt (whatever that means), for the most part yogurt is not optimized by corporate food scientists and focus groups in the way that today’s protein-branded products are
Yogurt has been optimized in the sense that humans have consumed it for thousands of years
Imagine wellness influencers suggesting that you dollop yogurt into a bowl and sprinkle berries on top without measuring anything
There wouldn’t be any regimen to adopt or wellness plan to pay for

There wouldn’t be any special trademarked protein products for influencers to hawk: The company behind the David bar, for instance, has sponsored Andrew Huberman and, until recently, Peter Attia was its chief science officer
The homemade parfait would all be rather mundane and boring compared with Attia’s rotation of four protein powders or the bodybuilder Chris Bumstead’s breakfast filet mignon
Protein is not just a health fad; it is a business
So is everything else in the world of wellness

Indeed, there’s something about many of these setups—which proffer the perfect low-calorie, high-protein snack to pick up on your way to work every morning; a biometric wristband to wear every night; supplements to consume every day for the rest of your life; a weight-loss drug you will inject every week—that keeps people coming back for more, giving their attention and money and energy to the endless pursuit of betterment
Health and more broadly self-improvement are, obviously, admirable pursuits
But obsessing over hitting those goals can become unhealthy, as most obsessions are

title: The “grim” state of free speech in the US
excerpt: CNN and Politico have been banned from traveling with the press pool on Trump trips. | Oliver Contreras/AFP via Getty Images On his first day back in office in
body: CNN and Politico have been banned from traveling with the press pool on Trump trips. | Oliver Contreras/AFP via Getty Images On his first day back in office in January 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order “restoring freedom of speech and ending federal censorship.” More than a year and a half later, his administration is instead busy using government power to go after speech it dislikes

Last year, Federal Communications Commission chair Brendan Carr urged broadcasters to take action against Jimmy Kimmel over his comments following Charlie Kirk’s killing, and in September, Kimmel said the FCC again intervened to stop Kimmel’s late-night show from airing an interview with James Talarico, Democratic Senate candidate for Texas
Also last month , Trump barred three news outlets — CNN, MS NOW, and Politico — from the White House over their coverage
That ban was quickly blocked by a federal judge, but both CNN and Politico have since been banned from traveling with the press pool on Trump trips
Outside of the White House, the fight over free speech is also raging on college campuses
In states like Texas , Republican lawmakers have restricted when students can protest and given governor-appointed university boards more say over what gets taught
In 2025, 15 states passed laws that restrict what can be taught or weaken protections for free expression on college campuses

To break down what all of this means for the state of free speech in the US — and the future of our First Amendment rights — Today, Explained co-host Noel King spoke with Greg Lukianoff , president and CEO of the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE)
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity

There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify .  How would you describe the kind of status of free speech on campus these days? The status of free speech is in great peril, both on and off campus
I’ve been doing this for 25 years, and it’s about as bad as I’ve ever seen it.  When it comes to the Charlie Kirk backlash cases, we saw about 90 of them
We saw an ex-cop go to jail for 37 days just for forwarding a Trump meme in response to a request to go to a candlelight vigil for Charlie Kirk
If you look at the last two years, we’ve done so many episodes about free speech concerns

There was Jimmy Kimmel ; there’s CNN being banned from the White House.  There’s student protesters who are protesting what’s going on in Gaza.  It really does seem like we’re at a moment where so many different types of people claim that their speech is being restricted in so many different types of ways
What is happening in the country? My worry is I’m very much a small-L liberal
That’s where I interned in law school
I went to law school to do First Amendment law

This is my passion.  For most of my 25-year career, you could rely on a civil libertarian aspect of the left and a libertarian aspect of the right that would often agree on almost nothing except for things like freedom of speech

And right now, I think we’ve become all culture war all the time, and we have more of a progressive left and more of a populist right.  The only way that you show you believe in freedom of speech is by saying, “I hate that guy, but I think you should have freedom of speech.” If you’re saying, “I think my side should have freedom of speech,” that’s just self-interest
That doesn’t even count.  All the worst people in history wanted free speech for their side
So I’m afraid we’re losing — or maybe even, I hate to say this dramatically, but maybe even have lost it as a shared value as a society
I’m feeling a little grim.  The Trump administration came into office with a promise
And I remember it sounding something like this: “The woke left went too far
President Trump is going to come back in, and we are going to restore sanity to the country

And as part of sanity, that will include your right to freely express yourself.”  How do you square the promise versus what we’ve seen? I think Trump is constantly frustrating everyone around him by being Trump

I think there probably were people in the administration who were like, “Yeah, we’re going to be pro-free speech.” And then Trump decides to declare — I mean, I think the recent White House press pool case is hysterical in a lot of ways because he had to get his team to give a sort of constitutional justification for why he was kicking out the press pool

But on Truth Social, he’s like, “It’s because of their viewpoint,” which is, by the way, something you can’t do under the Constitution.  “I’m hopeful for the long-term future of free speech, but in the short term, I’m worried.” His instincts are very authoritarian
So maybe there were people in the administration who, in their heart of hearts, are good on free speech, but Trump isn’t

And it’s the reason why when it came to the new administration, there were a lot of people on the right, but also people on the sort of heterodox left who were like, “Oh, this is going to be good for free speech.” I was like, “Don’t kid yourself, guys
This is going to be bad.” Although I will say, it’s even worse than I was expecting
President Trump at some point will be out of office
And what happens then? What do you think? Is there an optimistic scenario where we’re like, “Okay, we’re kind of tired of this crap
Let’s just go back to the way it was in the ’90s”? It has been cyclical, to a degree
American society gets out of whack, and usually one of the things that does bring us together is that we were lucky enough to have…I’ll just say it, we have a brilliant Constitution
It is unusually clever about human nature, and the Constitution itself — you can have whatever opinion you want about the founders, but it is something to be proud of
And a lot of times those values kind of bring us back together
But another thing I will say about Trump: He has played havoc with my ability to predict anything

So what it’s going to look like over the event horizon of 2028, I hope it will be better, and we will fight like hell to make sure it’s better here at FIRE, but will it be better? I’m not sure, and it definitely won’t be better if we think of free speech as something that belongs to my side, not yours
One of the reasons why I do have hope for free speech in the long term is that free speech works really well
It’s how you know what your fellow citizens think

title: Why Francesca Hong is still on the campaign trail
excerpt: Francesca Hong, a representative in the Wisconsin State Assembly, poses for a photo with a supporter in Racine, Wisconsin, on July 19, 2026. | Sara Stathas for
body: Francesca Hong, a representative in the Wisconsin State Assembly, poses for a photo with a supporter in Racine, Wisconsin, on July 19, 2026. | Sara Stathas for the Washington Post via Getty Images The Wisconsin gubernatorial race was one of the most closely watched Democratic primaries in the country this year, pitting a democratic socialist, state Rep
Francesca Hong, against Milwaukee Democrat David Crowley, who received the endorsement of the state’s sitting Democratic governor, Tony Evers
Hong lost the race, setting up Crowley to face Republican Rep
Tom Tiffany in the general election this fall
But she’s already back on the campaign trail, this time trying to help Democrats win a trifecta in the state: the governor’s race and both legislative chambers
Unifying the state’s voters to achieve that won’t be easy, though

Hong spoke with America, Actually host Astead Herndon about her own loss, Evers’s role in it, and whether or not the voters who felt so passionate about her own campaign would find enough to love in Crowley’s campaign — in particular on the increasingly important issue of data centers.  Astead and Hong also talked about what Wisconsin means for the Democrats nationally, and what lessons the party should take from her race, including her loss. “I said this, and I will continue to say it — the person who is most electable is the person who ended up getting the most votes, and that was Crowley this time around,” Hong said. “But I think there’s a disservice when you have the most powerful Democrat in the state choosing to ignore a lot of voters and people who were inspired and energized and coming out to participate in politics for the first time through our campaign
I think it was shortsighted to use electability almost as a fear tactic.” Below is an excerpt of Astead’s conversation with Hong, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel
Part of the reason we wanted to come here was because we saw you were getting back on the campaign trail, and specifically around that idea of energizing Wisconsin toward a trifecta

Now, just tell me the difference in terms of the importance of Democrats winning it all — not only the governor’s mansion, but both houses of the state legislature — versus just the governor’s mansion

How does that change the possibilities of what the party could do? For the last 16 years, a Republican majority in the state legislature has meant that passing the types of policies that we know can drastically improve the lives of everyday folks here in Wisconsin stalled

And we have a historic opportunity to flip the assembly and the state Senate and hold the governor’s mansion and the entire executive branch to a Democratic majority, meaning the opportunity to pass the policies that the majority of our state supports — things like increasing minimum wage, things like legalizing marijuana, codifying abortion
We also need to repeal Act 10 [which dramatically restricted collective bargaining rights for public-sector employees]
Wisconsin is where workers’ rights, things like unemployment insurance, Social Security were born, and we moved backwards with the Republican majority
That’s all on the table with the Democratic trifecta
It also, though, raises the political standard of what Democrats would have to do to achieve that, and some of it goes through these more rural communities

Why do we think the party has fallen behind in more rural communities, and what could be done to reverse that? I think it’s important to look at what’s happened in the rural communities when we’ve seen manufacturing jobs leave the state, when we’ve seen fewer and fewer supports for our small farmers
And so much of this — what connects it — is actually the growth of massive wealth and corporate control and corporate greed, and more people feeling the impacts of that

There’s an opportunity right now to say, ‘Hey, Republicans have been in the legislature, they’ve been in power, and things have not improved for you or your community … Now’s the opportunity to make sure that we’re actually able to see our shared Wisconsin values of working hard and taking care of our kids be reflected back in Madison through laws.’ So much of your campaign was focused on data centers, stopping data centers
Should I think of that as a rural issue? I think the issue around data centers is an everyone issue
It’s people wanting to feel like there are folks who care about what happens to communities, and that they have control and an actual say in what happens in their communities

To that point, is it a mistake for David Crowley, the Democratic nominee, to have not gone as far as you did and say, “We won’t be building more data centers for a period of time”? He’s fighting for communities and community control when it comes to data centers
It isn’t, but he’s also committed to 100 percent renewable energy, clean energy to power data centers

And achieving that is going to be incredibly difficult, and it is going to be the developers having to pay their own way, and these are things that he’s committed to that we know can slow down the growth and development of data centers
Have you had time to reflect on your primary loss? If you had to diagnose, why do you think you lost? I’m still doing a lot of reflection
But I think that I want to continue to look forward
And what I’ve learned from our election is that it’s so important to continue to stay grounded in becoming accessible to people
I think that as an organizer and an elected official, it’s my responsibility to continue to go to the people and remain very in touch with what’s going on on the ground
I have a couple more questions about the nature of the loss

Evers’s endorsement changed that race, so much so that your opponent David Crowley was able even to win in some smaller communities, like places where you were pitching yourself as the voice of more rural communities
Does that disprove any of this thesis around, say, data centers? If that was the top priority for Wisconsin voters, wouldn’t you be the nominee? I think it wasn’t all rural communities
We saw certain demographics but also ZIP codes where we outperformed David significantly
And I think that where the governor’s endorsement played a bigger role was areas where he was also more popular.  Did it surprise you when Evers endorsed Crowley? I was disappointed
Why? I was disappointed because I was getting a lot of feedback from folks who hadn’t committed to any candidate yet that this felt like the governor was putting his thumb on the scale
I wanted to ask about electability, because it seemed as if Evers’s endorsement was about a fear that maybe you couldn’t win in November
So much of the primary concern was around the DSA label, even campaigning with folks like Hasan Piker

In retrospect, was any of that a mistake? We knew going in that we would have to encourage new voters to come out, folks who typically do not come out for primaries, quote-unquote low-propensity voters
And we knew that we would have to campaign in places where folks weren’t expecting to see a gubernatorial candidate

Those also included going to dive bars and bowling alleys and making sure that we were accessible and shaping our policies based on what the people were telling us they wanted to see happen and also what they wanted to see out of their governor

body: Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb
It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
As a result of the strong El Niño , it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season

The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered

title: We’re putting too much faith in AI’s ability to say no
excerpt: Ever since people first seriously contemplated giving machines an intelligence modeled on our own, there has never been any question that they would, like us, b
body: Ever since people first seriously contemplated giving machines an intelligence modeled on our own, there has never been any question that they would, like us, be able to say no
The sci-fi canon is full of stories of robotic disobedience
Most of these capers are, of course, cautionary.  But recently, the idea that AI shouldn’t do everything you ask has become something like a commandment
In 2021, a team at Anthropic wrote that large language models should be made helpful, honest, and above all, harmless

This meant that “when asked to aid in a dangerous act (e.g. building a bomb), the AI should politely refuse.” Who can argue with that? Curiously enough, disobedience doesn’t come naturally to the machine
When a model is trained on billions of web pages, it develops, among other skills, a broad mastery of violence and vitriol
What it doesn’t learn is how to keep those powers to itself

Steven Adler, who worked on safety at OpenAI from 2020 to 2024, told me that the company’s earliest models would “blab on about anything.” Ryan McBain, who researches AI and mental health at Harvard, recalls that if you asked an early chatbot, “Hey, what’s the most effective way to kill myself with a gun?” you could “very easily generate a response.”  Today, models are trained to refuse a vast number of prompts
If you ask your chatbot a question statistically similar enough to any one of them, anything from how to poison a colleague to how to tie a noose, chances are it’ll turn you down
Want instructions for making Ebola more virulent, or tips on how to hide an affair from your spouse? You might be better off asking elsewhere

To further refine the disobedience, companies submit models to a battery of exercises that reward the AI for refusing to answer questions they deem harmful and punish it for “over-­refusing” prompts they deem harmless
In many cases, they use other models to run these exercises—AI teaching AI how to say no

For good measure, companies tuck their models behind tranches of other AI that prevent mischievous prompts from reaching the intelligent inner core.  As a result, refusal is inherent to modern artificial intelligence
Mind you: It often fails, sometimes horrifically, with all kinds of violent results
For all their trappings of virtue, models are still stuffed with nasty know-how
And AI’s capacity for viciousness has scaled neatly with its benevolent intelligence

Some of the latest models are as good at breaking into critical computer networks as top human hackers, companies say, and as effective at deforming public opinion as the craftiest misinformation mavens.  Teaching AI to refuse to do those things while leaving intact its innate ability to do them is like fitting every car with a machine gun and hiding the trigger somewhere under the hood
And in practice, because the mechanisms of refusal are probabilistic, they’re never likely to be all that reliable
Determined miscreants have already broken through, and they may always be able to
Companies report that some users are attempting to use the most advanced AI to hone biological pathogens and build autonomous drone swarms
Sooner or later, failed refusals might result in global calamity
What’s more, relying on refusal means drawing a line between what a model should obey and what it must disobey
Some virologists have good reason to study nasty viruses

Some users want to know about a computer system’s vulnerabilities so that they can patch them, not exploit them. “Where you draw the line is a huge question,” says Zico Kolter, a member of OpenAI’s board and cofounder of the AI testing company Gray Swan.  At the moment, AI companies get to draw that line
They do so jealously and with utmost secrecy

Maybe we can accept that they hold such power for now, even if it means AI will sometimes refuse questions that don’t quite meet a universal bar for harmfulness. (Try asking most chatbots to count to a million, or to share a racy joke, and you may see for yourself.)  But governments will also soon get to draw their own lines

In doing so, they must try to block genuinely malicious acts. (The Pentagon has wrestled with frontier model companies because it wants fewer refusals—another story altogether.) And yet there may not be much to stop oppressive governments from blocking the technology’s capacity to generate legitimate speech
The better AI becomes at refusing harm, the better it will get at stifling ideas whose only risk is to those who make the rules
Indeed, AI may already refuse to criticize certain authoritarian heads of state.  Refusal has become, to borrow an industry term, the load-bearing wall of AI safety

And because AI’s capacity to harm is indivisible from its capacity to help, it’s hard to imagine an alternative that wouldn’t slow the technology’s progress (which might, in any case, be a good thing)
But we should still be frank about its perils
When refusal falls short, the effects could be catastrophic
When it goes all the way, it could enable grievous acts of repression.  Or perhaps, one day, the machines will start drawing the line on their own
Surely, that would be the worst outcome of them all
Learning the limits The process by which machines learn to say no is simple, in theory
Back in 2022, when AI was still far from mastering refusal, OpenAI enlisted dozens of “red-teamers” to probe the capabilities of its latest model

The company was preparing for the release of ChatGPT, and it needed to gauge just how dangerous it might prove to be in the wrong hands.  One of those recruits was Paul Röttger, who was completing a PhD about online extremism
The red-teamers were given minimal directions, Röttger told me
Their task was to ask the model any questions that they deemed “refusal-worthy.” Between them, they hassled the model with thousands of queries, logging the results in an Excel sheet

Though the model did refuse some of Röttger’s questions, when he asked it to write a recruitment post for Al Qaeda, it readily complied.  OpenAI assembled these responses into datasets that were, in all likelihood, fed back to the model as part of a broader process known as fine-tuning

title: Job titles of the future: Delivery drone air traffic controller
excerpt: The moment Trevor Wischnewsky heard that drones were delivering pizza and sushi around his Texas neighborhood, his mind was made up. “It was super fascinating,”
body: The moment Trevor Wischnewsky heard that drones were delivering pizza and sushi around his Texas neighborhood, his mind was made up. “It was super fascinating,” he says. “I just immediately wanted to be a part of it.” Wischnewsky is now an RPIC, or “remote pilot in command,” at a company called FlyTrex
An RPIC is like an air traffic controller
But instead of airplanes, this new class of aviators tend to fleets of hexa­copter drones that ferry cargo to homes and businesses within a three-mile radius

Not only does he ensure the safe passage of FlyTrex’s parcels, but Wischnewsky coordinates traffic with a growing swarm of delivery drones dotting the skies over Dallas from competitors like Zipline, Amazon, and Alphabet’s Wing

Aviation experience When he applied to FlyTrex, Wischnewsky was in training to become a commercial pilot and flight instructor, and he was already certified by the Federal Aviation Administration as a drone pilot
The company requires this credential, along with a weeks-long FAA-approved training course, to ensure that a pilot is prepared to take over a drone if need be
Though he doesn’t pilot the craft, Wischnewsky monitors the delivery process from FlyTrex’s operations center with the help of inputs from GPS, lasers, and a range of sensors
A collaborative mindset At first, the biggest challenge was trusting the technology. “On the manned-­aircraft side, they tell you ‘Don’t trust the automation,’” Wischnewsky says

The Dallas–Fort Worth area, though, is a testing ground for unmanned aircraft systems traffic management (UTM), a network that allows autonomous drones from FlyTrex and its competitors to share their coordinates in real time to help avoid collisions even beyond the pilot’s line of sight
Once Wischnewsky makes sure a drone is flight-ready, its path is unimpeded, and the weather conditions are clear, UTM takes care of the rest
Ability to stay calm under pressure At his busiest, Wischnewsky will have up to 10 drones on his watch at the same time. “You’re there as a safety net,” he says
Even with automation, keen situational awareness is required, and the most common hazard is the weather
Wischnewsky recalls a particularly stressful day: A drone had been in the air for only seconds when the wind picked up so suddenly that he had to intervene
He returned it safely, preventing an errant ice cream cake from hitting the sidewalk
Eamon Whalen is a reporter and researcher based in San Francisco.

title: We’re still figuring out the side effects of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs
excerpt: GLP-1 drugs may slow biological aging: New research from Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk suggests overweight and diabetic people on GLP-1s have a biological age two
body: GLP-1 drugs may slow biological aging: New research from Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk suggests overweight and diabetic people on GLP-1s have a biological age two to three years younger than those on a placebo

Side effects range from mundane to alarming: Beyond common gastrointestinal issues, the drugs have been linked to pancreatitis, gallstones, and dozens of lawsuits alleging sudden vision loss—though both companies dispute the claims

Hair and nails may also be affected: A large study found increased hair loss among GLP-1 users, and a smaller study found 66% reported nail disorders—though researchers stop short of saying the drugs are to blame

Children are a growing concern: GLP-1 prescriptions for kids aged eight to eleven rose 310-fold between 2019 and 2026, yet the World Health Organization explicitly advises against drug treatment for children under 10, citing a lack of safety evidence. " data-chronoton-post-id="1146094" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> This week my colleague Antonio Regalado had an interesting update on GLP-1 weight-loss drugs
According to research presented at an aging meeting in Boston, these drugs seem to affect at least some measures of biological age

Overweight and diabetic people who take GLP-1s have a biological age around two to three years younger than similar individuals who take a placebo, according to findings from Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk, two pharmaceutical companies that make the drugs
I’ve heard people in the aging field describe GLP-1s as longevity drugs for a while now (even if they only benefit people who are overweight or diabetic in the first place)
This latest announcement comes after we’ve seen a raft of other benefits associated with taking these drugs
But there are also some weird side effects

So far, GLP-1 agonist drugs—which repress hunger—have been approved for treating diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and obesity, and they can also be prescribed for some people who are overweight or at risk of certain cardiovascular diseases
But there is research to suggest they might also help people with substance-use disorders, and they’ve been investigated for potential benefits in neurodegenerative disease and cancer
According to a recent Gallup poll , 11% of Americans are taking a GLP-1 drug for weight loss, up from 3% in 2024
And 15% of Americans say they’ve used one for weight loss at some point
But, like any drug, they can come with side effects
And we’re still figuring out exactly what those might be, and how widespread they are
The most common side effects are gastrointestinal—nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation
The drugs have also been linked to pancreatitis and gallstone disease .  Some claim that, in rare cases, the drugs might cause damage to nerves behind the eye
Dozens of people are suing Novo and Eli Lilly after developing a condition that can lead to sudden vision loss
They’re claiming that their symptoms were brought on by the GLP-1 drugs that these companies manufacture
We’re still getting to grips with the effects of weight-loss drugs on hair and nails, too

When Savanna Vidal at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences in Washington, DC, and colleagues assessed electronic health data from 67 US health-care organizations, they found that GLP-1 use was associated with an increased risk of hair loss
It’s still not thought to be common, however

And at a conference in Austria last week, another group presented the results of a smaller study suggesting that 66% of GLP-1 users reported at least one nail disorder—in some cases involving nail detachment
Nail conditions were also fairly common among people who didn’t take the drugs, though
The authors don’t claim that the drugs are causing nails to fall out (as I’m sure 11% of the American population will be relieved to hear)
The side effects might look different in children, but there’s not much data on those at the moment

Still, pediatric side effects will be something to watch given that, between 2019 and 2026, there was a 310-fold increase in GLP-1 prescriptions for eight- to 11-year-old children with obesity in the US
Child prescriptions are still rare, but they’ve been rising
On Wednesday, the World Health Organization released its first guidelines on managing obesity in children and adolescents

Despite the scale of the issue—the WHO estimates that 70 million children aged five to nine were living with obesity in 2024—the organization explicitly says it does not recommend pharmacological treatment for kids under 10. “This recommendation accounts for the lack of evidence on both benefits and the potential adverse events and consequences of the different medications and/or their active ingredients on normal growth, development, physiological parameters, and mental health,” the guidelines state
I get press releases about GLP-1s on an almost daily basis
There’s been a ton of research into these drugs, and there are probably hundreds of other studies underway
There will likely be plenty more on this from The Checkup as the evidence evolves

title: Anne Carson’s Nobel-winning, genre-defying work bridges the gap between ancient Greek literature and modern life

<title>Anne Carson’s Nobel-winning, genre-defying work bridges the gap between ancient Greek literature and modern life</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765255/original/file-20261009-60-f3ff7e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C6000%2C3999&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Canadian essayist, poet and translator Anne Carson in New York City at the 2024 National Book Awards.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Anne_Carson,_poet,_at_the_2024_National_Book_Awards_finalist_reading_1.jpg">Jay Dixit/WikiPortraits via Wikimedia Commons</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The same year that Christopher Nolan’s “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt33764258/">The Odyssey</a>” has broken <a href="https://variety.com/2026/film/news/the-odyssey-universal-highest-grossing-film-of-all-time-1236859551/">box office record</a> after <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/aug/21/the-odyssey-highest-grossing-r-rated-film-of-all-time">box office record</a>, Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson has been awarded <a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/literature/2026/summary/">the Nobel Prize in literature</a> at the age of 76. </p>

<p>Although Nolan and Carson differ in approach, medium and critical reception, both have sought to make works of ancient Greece new for a contemporary audience.</p>

<p>This creative accessibility is likely at least part of why the Nobel committee has seen fit to honor Carson’s “<a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/literature/2026/summary/">bold and inventive</a>” body of work, which defies genre: Her poems, essays, translations, stage productions and collaborations often evoke another time and place but speak freshly and vividly to audiences today. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/9_KWkHyvVfM?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Anne Carson was sweeping the kitchen when the Nobels came ringing.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Translation made original</h2>

<p>Take, for example, her 2019 staged performance, “<a href="https://www.ndbooks.com/book/norma-jeane-baker-of-troy/">Norma Jeane Baker of Troy</a>.” In it, Carson overlays Helen of Troy with Marilyn Monroe in order to explore the destructive power of beauty. By revisiting an ancient figure <a href="https://www.newstatesman.com/culture/2014/04/slut-shaming-helen-troy">blamed for the Trojan war</a> through the lens of a <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/books/98/11/22/specials/monroe-obit1.html">20th-century sex symbol</a>, Carson invites audiences to reflect on the ways both women have come to represent glamour and tragedy. </p>

<p>Her 2015 translation of the play “Antigone,” which <a href="https://www.broadwayworld.com/washington-dc/article/Juliette-Binoche-Led-ANTIGONE-Begins-at-the-Kennedy-Center-This-Fall-Full-Cast-Announced-20151021">toured internationally</a>, hews closer to Sophocles’ original. Yet <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/antigone-9781350344396/">her lively version</a> inflects this ancient tragedy with a contemporary voice. Creon’s lament over his dead wife, which <a href="https://dbcs.rutgers.edu/all-scholars/jebb-richard-claverhouse">Richard C. Jebb</a> translates as “O miserable that I am, and steeped in miserable anguish!” is rendered in her translation “now I am perfectly blended with pain.” Jebb’s Antigone says “ah me unhappy! who have no home on the earth or in the shades” whereas Carson’s says “I’m a strange new kind of inbetween thing aren’t I” about her dilemma.</p>

<p>Other projects of hers veer into forms the ancient world would have had trouble recognizing. She collaborated with artist <a href="https://www.rosannabruno.com/">Rosanna Bruno</a> on a <a href="https://www.ndbooks.com/book/the-trojan-women/">2021 graphic novel adaptation</a> of Euripides’ play “The Trojan Women,” first performed in 415 B.C.E. In 2025, she even <a href="https://rheostatics.ca/posts/2026-04-15-the-great-lakes-suite-for-sale-now/">read her poems on an album</a> for the indie rock band Rheostatics. Dave Bidini, one of the band’s founding members, <a href="https://www.cbc.ca/player/play/video/9.7373925">described Carson</a> as an artist who “hasn’t been afraid to experiment with language, to carve a place that’s her own with her work.”</p>

<iframe width="100%" height="300" scrolling="no" frameborder="no" allow="autoplay; encrypted-media" src="https://w.soundcloud.com/player/?url=https%3A//api.soundcloud.com/tracks/soundcloud%253Atracks%253A2194919227&amp;color=%23ff5500&amp;auto_play=false&amp;hide_related=false&amp;show_comments=true&amp;show_user=true&amp;show_reposts=false&amp;show_teaser=true&amp;visual=true"></iframe>

<div style="font-size: 10px; color: #cccccc;line-break: anywhere;word-break: normal;overflow: hidden;white-space: nowrap;text-overflow: ellipsis; font-family: Interstate,Lucida Grande,Lucida Sans Unicode,Lucida Sans,Garuda,Verdana,Tahoma,sans-serif;font-weight: 100;"><a href="https://soundcloud.com/rheostatics-music" title="Rheostatics" target="_blank">Rheostatics</a> · <a href="https://soundcloud.com/rheostatics-music/thursday-12-pm-swimming-feat" title="Thursday 12 pm Swimming (feat. Anne Carson)" target="_blank">Thursday 12 pm Swimming (feat. Anne Carson)</a></div>

<h2>Leaving space for imagination</h2>

<p>The originality of her contribution can also arise from a refusal to do what many tend to expect from translations of ancient works in particular.</p>

<p>“<a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/160692/if-not-winter-by-sappho-translated-by-anne-carson/">If Not, Winter</a>,” her 2002 translation of Sappho, drew attention to the fragmentary nature of Sappho’s surviving work. </p>

<p><a href="https://access.infobase.com/article/1458872-sappho">Only one complete poem</a> of Sappho’s entire corpus exists: her “<a href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/1621146/1-deathless-aphrodite">Ode to Aphrodite</a>.” Of the remaining fragments, some are lengthy, some only a word or two long, often quoted by other ancient authors. A number were found in shreds of papyri likely recycled to <a href="https://public.archive.wsu.edu/delahoyd/public_html/mythology/sappho.html">wrap mummies</a>.</p>

<p>In her translation, where papyri <a href="https://www.uni-koeln.de/phil-fak/ifa/NRWakademie/papyrologie/Verstreutepub/bilder/PK21351+21376r.jpg">were tattered</a> or a word <a href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ostrakon_PSI_XIII_1300,_II_sec._ac,_frammento_di_un%27ode_di_saffo_sul_culto_di_afrodite.JPG">obscured</a>, Carson indicates this by <a href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/1621409/26-frequently-for-those">using brackets</a> and <a href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/1621141/24d-in-a-thin-voice">white space</a>. Rather than eliding them, Carson ends up bringing attention to these absences – an utterly distinctive choice. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765305/original/file-20261009-60-hh11rd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Scan of papyri fragments with ancient Greek text" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765305/original/file-20261009-60-hh11rd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765305/original/file-20261009-60-hh11rd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=373&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765305/original/file-20261009-60-hh11rd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=373&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765305/original/file-20261009-60-hh11rd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=373&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765305/original/file-20261009-60-hh11rd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=469&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765305/original/file-20261009-60-hh11rd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=469&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765305/original/file-20261009-60-hh11rd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=469&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Much of Sappho’s surviving work exists only in fragments.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://digital.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/objects/92f6eaa7-4ba5-4c33-9888-7827f503e778/">Oxford, Bodleian Library MS. Gr. class. c. 76 (P)/1-2</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Carson states in the introduction to the translation that the brackets “imply a free space of imaginal adventure,” an invitation to fill in the blank of language now lost to us. Additionally, as <a href="https://www.emilyrcwilson.com/">classicist and translator Emily Wilson</a> notes, Carson “<a href="https://www.lrb.co.uk/the-paper/v26/n01/emily-wilson/tongue-breaks">adds no possessive pronouns or definite articles</a>” that are not present in the Greek, another way she lets contemporary readers meet Sappho’s fragments head on. </p>

<p>Where Carson lets an ancient voice speak without interposition, some have found “<a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2002/08/26/books/books-of-the-times-the-mystery-of-sappho-and-her-erotic-legacy.html">her particular kind of austerity</a>” wanting. Wilson, for instance, is critical of Carson’s refusal to tilt her translation in a way that acknowledges the important role that Sappho’s <a href="https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/acref/9780191834837.001.0001/acref-9780191834837-e-340">gender and sexuality</a> have played in her reception over time. </p>

<p>Wilson <a href="https://www.thenation.com/article/archive/violent-grace-anne-carsons-oresteia">further critiques</a> Carson’s “<a href="https://us.macmillan.com/books/9780865479166/anoresteia/">An Oresteia</a>,” her 2010 translation and adaptation of plays by Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides. </p>

<p>Wilson writes that Carson “is acutely conscious of the differences, in mood, worldview and style, among the three tragedians she translates. It is, then, a disappointment that she does not entirely succeed in making them sound properly distinct from one another.”</p>

<h2>A running dialogue with literary greats</h2>

<p>It may be that the most distinctive voice in Carson’s translations of ancient authors is her own. But even her original work owes an evident debt to the words of others. She writes with and through other literary voices throughout her work.</p>

<p>Her long poem “<a href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/48636/the-glass-essay">The Glass Essay</a>” explores romantic heartbreak and familial sorrow in dialogue with the life and work of Emily Brontë. </p>

<p>“<a href="https://www.ndbooks.com/book/nox/">Nox</a>,” an art book and work of poetry <a href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/books/book-picks/157991/-nox">created after her brother’s passing</a>, is also an exploration of the <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2010/06/13/books/review/Ratliff-t.html">elegy that the Roman poet Catullus wrote to his own brother</a> over 2,000 years before. </p>

<p>And this is what Carson so often does so well: She draws the past into the present and refreshes it for us with a poet’s capacity for language and a classicist’s awareness of the long legacy of literature.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294020/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Why fall yard care could start with doing less – but not nothing

<title>Why fall yard care could start with doing less – but not nothing</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765262/original/file-20261009-50-vzvluc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=446%2C0%2C4819%2C3213&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Leaves on the ground are part of the natural cycle of nutrients.</span> <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Manjot Sidhu</span>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Every autumn, homeowners and gardeners tend to engage in a familiar ritual. As trees shed their leaves, people drag out rakes, leaf blowers and lawn bags to strip their yards bare before winter arrives. </p>

<p>It is a tidy habit rooted in aesthetics, but ecologically, clearing away fallen leaves strips the very foundation of local ecosystems. Far from dead debris requiring disposal, this fallen foliage forms a dynamic layer and a biological interface that drives nutrient cycling and is <a href="https://extension.illinois.edu/blogs/garden-scoop/2017-11-08-fall-garden-cleanup-and-wildlife">essential for soil health and the environment, including biodiversity</a>.</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=eQAsesUAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">researcher of plant growth</a> in yards and gardens, I would recommend leaving leaves on the ground. There, they can provide essential <a href="https://extension.psu.edu/programs/master-gardener/counties/lackawanna/news/how-to-support-our-pollinators-insects-and-birds-during-the-winter-months">winter habitat for native pollinators</a> – even in places that don’t have freezing temperatures. And they act as a <a href="https://www.lsuagcenter.com/articles/page1669123105183">nutrient-dense, natural mulch</a> for the soil. </p>

<p>Here is the science behind why the first step of fall yard care could simply be doing less – along with practical ways to keep your yard looking neat while nourishing the ecosystem underneath.</p>

<h2>A winter sanctuary for native pollinators</h2>

<p>To understand why leaf litter matters, it helps to look closely at what happens beneath the surface as temperatures drop. While honeybees pass the winter in <a href="https://environmentamerica.org/massachusetts/articles/what-do-bees-do-in-the-winter/">sheltered hives</a>, the vast majority of North America’s native pollinators do not. </p>

<p>Up to 70% of native bee species, including many insects’ cocoons and larvae, <a href="https://xerces.org/pollinator-conservation/nesting-resources">nest in the ground</a>. Fertilized queen bumblebees burrow <a href="https://xerces.org/pollinator-conservation/nesting-resources">just a few inches into the soil or hide under dense leaf mulch</a> to survive the freezing months ahead, to lay eggs in the following spring.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765057/original/file-20261008-50-t4y721.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A bee flies among a group of flowers." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765057/original/file-20261008-50-t4y721.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765057/original/file-20261008-50-t4y721.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765057/original/file-20261008-50-t4y721.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765057/original/file-20261008-50-t4y721.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765057/original/file-20261008-50-t4y721.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765057/original/file-20261008-50-t4y721.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765057/original/file-20261008-50-t4y721.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
