              <span class="caption">If bees and other pollinators are to return in the spring, they need somewhere to shelter in the winter.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/los-angeles-ca-birds-eye-gilia-is-seen-in-the-yard-of-news-photo/2177502429">Dania Maxwell/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Raking, bagging and blowing leaves away destroys this crucial winter nursery.</p>

<p>Many other insects depend on the shelter of fallen foliage:</p>

<ul>
<li><p>Moths and butterflies: Species such as the <a href="https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/47916-Actias-luna">luna moth (<em>Actias luna</em>)</a> and the Isabella tiger moth, whose <a href="https://www.keystone.edu/2026/10/07/woolly-bears-on-campus-folklore-fall-and-the-facts/">caterpillar form is the woolly bear</a>, spin cocoons or roll themselves directly inside fallen leaves. Raking or shredding those leaves destroys the next generation.</p></li>
<li><p>Fireflies: Adult fireflies lay eggs in moist soil, and their larvae spend up to two years hunting for their food, <a href="https://blog.nwf.org/2024/09/leave-the-leaves-to-save-fireflies/">soft-bodied invertebrates under damp leaf litter</a>. Raking deprives them of moisture and habitat.</p></li>
<li><p><a href="https://ipm.ucanr.edu/natural-enemies/predaceous-ground-beetles/#gsc.tab=0">Predatory ground beetles</a>: These beneficial predators <a href="https://www.lsuagcenter.com/%7E/media/system/b/8/4/b/b84bc30880b73ecdd797defdedd2cec7/p3949%20maintainingleaflitter_rh924pdf.pdf">spend the winter under leaves</a>, emerging in spring to feed on common garden pests such as aphids, slugs and mites. </p></li>
</ul>

<h2>Nature’s engineered soil insulator and fertilizer</h2>

<p>In addition to being a shelter, <a href="https://njaes.rutgers.edu/fs1369/">fallen leaves are an evolved biological mechanism for nutrient cycling</a>. Trees actively pump vital elements, including calcium, magnesium, potassium and nitrogen from deep subsoils, into their foliage. When autumn comes and leaves drop, these stored nutrients are deposited back into the soil.</p>

<p>Leaving leaves in place triggers fundamental ecological benefits.</p>

<p>A thick blanket of intact leaves acts as a natural insulator for the ground. Air pockets trapped between overlapping leaves moderate the soil temperature and slow heat transfer, <a href="https://yardandgarden.extension.iastate.edu/faq/what-frost-heaving-and-how-do-i-prevent-it">buffering against the freeze-thaw cycles that heave soil</a>, fracture plant roots and expose beneficial soil microbes to lethal cold. The intact leaf blanket also conserves moisture and prevents soil from drying out over the winter.</p>

<p>As fungi, earthworms and micro-arthropods digest fallen leaves through late fall and spring, they <a href="https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/humus/">break down organic matter into a rich material called humus</a>. This slow-release organic fertilizer boosts soil structure, improves water retention in sandy soils, and <a href="https://wcsoilworks.com/humus-versatile-and-close-to-nature/">prevents erosion and runoff in heavy rains</a>.</p>

<p>Decaying leaves feed beneficial mycorrhizal fungi in the soil. Those fungi form <a href="https://njaes.rutgers.edu/FS1384/">symbiotic relationships with plant and tree roots</a>, helping the roots collect water and nutrients from the soil to nourish the plants above. A natural layer of leaves also <a href="https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/using-leaves-in-the-landscape/">suppresses spring weed seeds</a> organically without needing synthetic chemical herbicides. And the moist, insulated microclimate under leaf litter is also critical for <a href="https://njaes.rutgers.edu/fs1369/">terrestrial amphibians, including frogs and salamanders</a>, to survive freezing temperatures.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765059/original/file-20261008-70-iajxjh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Fallen leaves spread across a grassy area." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765059/original/file-20261008-70-iajxjh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765059/original/file-20261008-70-iajxjh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765059/original/file-20261008-70-iajxjh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765059/original/file-20261008-70-iajxjh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765059/original/file-20261008-70-iajxjh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765059/original/file-20261008-70-iajxjh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765059/original/file-20261008-70-iajxjh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Leaves can also harbor ticks, but if you move them to places people don’t frequent, even in the warmer months, you can reduce the number of ticks in places with activity.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/arcadia-ca-colorful-oak-leaves-line-the-pathways-at-the-los-news-photo/2186864492=">David Crane/MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>How to ‘leave the leaves’</h2>

<p>Adopting a softer approach to fall cleanup does not mean your yard has to look completely untamed or that you have to <a href="https://www.southernliving.com/hidden-dangers-leaves-lawn-12129619">risk killing your lawn</a>. Here is how to balance suburban expectations with sound ecological science:</p>

<ul>
<li><p>Move, don’t remove: Move the leaves from lawns and sidewalks, rake them into garden beds, around ornamental plants or into vegetable plots, using manual rakes or electric leaf blowers. Aim for a layer 2 to 3 inches deep. Leaving leaves in grassy areas can <a href="https://www.capecod.gov/2025/11/25/leave-the-leaves-cape-cod/">help ticks hide there too</a>, but if you move the leaves to garden beds or spots that are used less, the ticks will be less likely to nest in the grass. Establishing <a href="https://tickfreenh.org/reduce-ticks-while-supporting-pollinators-in-your-yard/">pollinator zones</a> on the property can also help reduce tick populations.</p></li>
<li><p>Skip the leaf shredder: Mowing over leaves with a mulching mower is better than sending them to landfills, but high-velocity mower blades still kill overwintering insect eggs, chrysalises and larvae. Leave leaves intact wherever possible in plant beds.</p></li>
<li><p>Wait for spring to clean up: Do not cut back hollow-stemmed perennials or clear leaf beds during early, warm spring days. Wait until temperatures consistently stay above 50 degrees Fahrenheit (10 degrees Celsius) so overwintering bees and butterflies <a href="https://engagement.source.colostate.edu/meant-to-bee-the-overwintering-strategies-of-bees-and-how-we-can-help/">have time to safely emerge</a>.</p></li>
</ul>

<p>When you bag leaves for disposal and then buy commercial wood mulch or synthetic fertilizers in the spring, you are effectively paying a price for what your trees provided for free. By rethinking the cultural expectation of pristine autumn lawns, it’s possible to transform silent landscapes into vibrant habitat sanctuaries, simply by stepping back and allowing natural processes to take over.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293924/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>How Hurricane Isaias broke through to become the first Atlantic hurricane in an extremely quiet 2026 season</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765357/original/file-20261010-50-mnsr8a.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=276%2C0%2C1853%2C1235&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Hurricane Isaias just after making landfall near Destin, Fla., on Oct. 9, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.star.nesdis.noaa.gov/goes/floater.php?stormid=AL092026#homePageLink">NOAA</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Hurricane Isaias shattered the peace of one of the quietest Atlantic hurricane seasons on record as it grew into <a href="https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/refresh/graphics_at4+shtml/080328.shtml?cone">2026’s first Atlantic hurricane</a> and <a href="https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2026/al09/al092026.update.10100129.shtml">made landfall on the northern Gulf Coast</a> near Destin, Fla., late on Oct. 9.</p>

<p>The Category 2 hurricane’s <a href="https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2026/al09/al092026.update.10100129.shtml">storm surge reached 5.6 feet</a> at nearby Panama City Beach as it crossed the coast. Forecasters warned of <a href="https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2026/al09/al092026.discus.013.shtml">damaging wind gusts</a> over a large portion of the
southeastern U.S. and flooding rain as the storm moved inland toward the Appalachian Mountains.</p>

<p>Isaias <a href="https://www.nesdis.noaa.gov/news/noaas-goes-east-satellite-monitors-hurricane-isaias">tied a 1905 storm</a> for the latest-forming first hurricane of a season on record. To understand why it was able to strengthen into a hurricane when no other storms in the first two-thirds of the 2026 season did, let’s take a look at what was going on in the atmosphere.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765014/original/file-20261008-60-y4cnum.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Hurricane Isaias moves through the central Gulf of Mexico. Most of its rain bands are to the northeast of the hurricane's eye." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765014/original/file-20261008-60-y4cnum.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765014/original/file-20261008-60-y4cnum.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=600&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765014/original/file-20261008-60-y4cnum.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=600&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765014/original/file-20261008-60-y4cnum.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=600&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765014/original/file-20261008-60-y4cnum.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=754&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765014/original/file-20261008-60-y4cnum.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=754&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765014/original/file-20261008-60-y4cnum.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=754&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Hurricane Isaias faced strong winds as it moved across warm Gulf waters. The wind influence is evidence in the storm’s lopsided rain bands, primarily pushed to its northeast, on Oct. 8, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.star.nesdis.noaa.gov/goes/index.php">NOAA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>As an <a href="https://www.umass.edu/engineering/news/davis-paros-chair">atmospheric scientist</a> who has studied hurricanes for years, I can tell you that wind shear and the climate phenomenon known as El Niño both play important roles.</p>

<h2>Why the 2026 season had such a quiet start</h2>

<p>Usually, Atlantic hurricane activity <a href="https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/climo/">hits its peak in September</a>. In a typical season, the Atlantic region experiences <a href="https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/climo/">five hurricanes and two major hurricanes</a> by early October. Having no hurricanes <a href="https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/refresh/graphics_at4+shtml/080328.shtml?cone">until Oct. 7</a> is nearly unprecedented in the Atlantic hurricane record.</p>

<p>The main culprit is likely El Niño.</p>

<p>El Niño is <a href="https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/ninonina.html">a climate pattern</a> that occurs every few years when ocean surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean heat up. That heat can influence weather around the world – including Atlantic hurricanes.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/WPA-KpldDVc?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">How El Niño influences weather around the world, including Atlantic hurricanes.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The 2026 <a href="https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso/roni/outlook/">El Niño was already strong</a> by late summer, and forecasters expected to see it become <a href="https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso_advisory/ensodisc.shtml">one of the strongest</a> El Niño events on record.</p>

<h2>2 ways El Niño prevents hurricanes from forming</h2>

<p>When the waters of the eastern Pacific warm substantially, they create more rising air over the eastern Pacific, and with it, more <a href="https://www.climate.gov/news-features/blogs/enso/walker-circulation-ensos-atmospheric-buddy">widespread thunderstorm activity</a>. The net effect is a current of rising air that flows northward across portions of Central America. This flow turns toward the east in the Northern Hemisphere <a href="https://www.nesdis.noaa.gov/about/k-12-education/atmosphere/what-the-coriolis-effect">because of the Earth’s rotation</a>, and it increases the westerly winds across the tropical Atlantic.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765018/original/file-20261008-50-ppox14.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Two illustrations show how El Niño shorts the air circulation to create conditions less conducive to Atlantic hurricanes." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765018/original/file-20261008-50-ppox14.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765018/original/file-20261008-50-ppox14.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=479&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765018/original/file-20261008-50-ppox14.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=479&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765018/original/file-20261008-50-ppox14.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=479&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765018/original/file-20261008-50-ppox14.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=602&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765018/original/file-20261008-50-ppox14.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=602&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765018/original/file-20261008-50-ppox14.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=602&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Under normal atmospheric circulation, air in the eastern tropical Pacific sinks, leaving drier air in that region, while the tropical Atlantic has moist, rising air that can fuel hurricanes. During El Niños, however, that flips – the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean is wetter, creating strongly rising air and more Pacific hurricanes, while the region where Atlantic hurricanes typically form is drier and less stormy.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.climate.gov/news-features/blogs/enso/walker-circulation-ensos-atmospheric-buddy">NOAA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Winds near the surface blowing from the east, along with winds at higher altitudes blowing from the west, create <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-is-wind-shear-an-atmospheric-scientist-explains-how-it-can-tear-apart-hurricanes-and-why-el-nino-ramps-it-up-213527">vertical wind shear</a>. Wind shear makes it harder for hurricanes to form because it disrupts any deep column of moisture that tries to organize into a vortex.</p>

<p>El Niño has another effect on Atlantic hurricane formation: With more rising air above the eastern Pacific warm waters, air tends to <a href="https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/el-nino-and-la-nina-frequently-asked-questions">subside over the tropical Atlantic and become dry</a>. Hurricanes need lots of moisture, so dry air makes it harder for one to form.</p>

<p>The tropical Atlantic was hit with both vertical wind shear and dry air in 2026.</p>

<p>Most of the <a href="https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/index.php">storms that managed to form</a> in the Atlantic earlier in 2026 did so to the north of the region of vertical shear and dry air, but it is rare for storms forming at those higher latitudes to become strong hurricanes.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765053/original/file-20261008-50-fldp6o.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A map shows all the storm tracks in 2026." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765053/original/file-20261008-50-fldp6o.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765053/original/file-20261008-50-fldp6o.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=446&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765053/original/file-20261008-50-fldp6o.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=446&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765053/original/file-20261008-50-fldp6o.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=446&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765053/original/file-20261008-50-fldp6o.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=560&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765053/original/file-20261008-50-fldp6o.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=560&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765053/original/file-20261008-50-fldp6o.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=560&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">The hurricane storm tracks in 2026, through Oct. 8, show that most storms formed in northern areas.             </figcaption>

<h2>How Isaias formed in these conditions</h2>

<p>So how did Isaias manage to break through?</p>

<p>First, Isaias did not form in the deep tropics, where many of the strongest hurricanes originate. That region is still seeing plenty of wind shear. Isaias <a href="https://www.yahoo.com/news/weather-news/articles/tropical-storm-isaias-formed-south-142516301.html">formed over the western Gulf</a> of Mexico (also referred to as the Gulf of America) instead. </p>

<p>In early October, <a href="https://www.atmos.albany.edu/student/abentley/realtime/standard.php?domain=northamer&amp;variable=irro_wind">vertical wind shear in the western Gulf weakened</a> and a small region of enhanced moisture moved over the western Gulf. Both of these factors made hurricane formation more likely, and <a href="https://theeyewall.substack.com/p/hurricane-isaias-is-strengthening">exceptionally warm</a> water provided fuel for the storm that formed.</p>

<p>Isaias organized rapidly in this environment.</p>

<p><iframe id="mP43e" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/mP43e/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Fifty years of Atlantic hurricane seasons show there have been just a few with only a couple of hurricanes forming."></iframe></p>

<p>But, as is often true with late-season hurricanes approaching the U.S., the jet stream is not far away. While Isaias strengthened, vertical shear also started increasing – not due to El Niño, but because the <a href="https://s.w-x.co/wxnext/img/SummertoFallJetStream.png">jet stream tends to dip farther south</a> as autumn sets in.</p>

<p>Isaias grew into a dangerous storm, but it could have been even stronger without the effects of wind shear.</p>



<h2>What’s ahead for Atlantic hurricane season?</h2>

<p>The rapid emergence of Isaias is a reminder that a slow start to the hurricane season doesn’t mean a quiet end. The season does not end officially until November 30.</p>

<p>Atmospheric conditions often change considerably in October from what they were in July through September as temperatures fall. So coastal regions can’t let their guard down yet – the season could bring more surprises.</p>

Ford arrives on May 16, 2026, in Norfolk, Va. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/person-waves-an-american-flag-as-aircraft-carrier-uss-news-photo/2275919031?phrase=mike kropf flag&amp;adppopup=true">Mike Kropf/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Where has more than seven months of <a href="https://theconversation.com/topics/iran-war-185765">intermittent war</a>, <a href="https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0613">economic threats</a>, <a href="https://apnews.com/article/iran-us-israel-trump-lebanon-march-24-2026-8bb5e79a98ea72fccc5c50b4931ad778">stalled diplomacy and promises of a ceasefire</a> in Iran left the concept of U.S. <a href="https://fpif.org/america-lacks-credibility-middle-east/">strategic credibility</a>?</p>

<p>It is a question that <a href="https://history.osu.edu/people/nichols.872">political scientists</a> and security and <a href="https://polisci.osu.edu/people/sarkar.115">foreign policy experts</a> like us have had to grapple with at each turn of the conflict.</p>

<p>Some <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2026/03/01/united-states-strikes-attack-iran-khamenei/">commentators have argued</a> that the bombings and multiple ceasefires actually strengthen American credibility by demonstrating American deterrence capabilities and resolve toward adversaries.</p>

<p><a href="https://thehill.com/opinion/international/5764825-the-world-is-watching-america-lose-its-moral-compass-and-its-global-credibility/">Others cite</a> the lack of a persuasive justification for conflict, the strikes themselves and subsequent fits and starts of peacemaking as evidence that America’s global image has been undermined, as has the persuasiveness of its public claims. And this, in turn, has undercut the credibility of future pronouncements by the U.S. administration. </p>

<p>Either way, <a href="https://www.wsj.com/opinion/american-credibility-is-on-the-line-in-iran-84c13e6a">most observers insist</a> that for the United States, “credibility is on the line in Iran.” But that has long been a central concern of U.S. foreign policy. As political scientist Stephen Walt observed in 2022, one of the most predictable aspects of virtually any debate over Washington’s involvement overseas is the “<a href="https://foreignpolicy.com/2022/01/29/us-credibility-ukraine-russia-grand-strategy/">ritual invoking of ‘credibility</a>.’” </p>

<p>But what, exactly, is “American credibility”? And why is there apparently so much groupthink about the concept and practice?</p>

<h2>Vietnam and the credibility discourse</h2>

<p>For policymakers, diplomats and scholars the technical definition is straightforward: Credibility refers to the perceived likelihood that a country will reliably keeps its promises, carry out its threats and deliver on its pledges. In this manner, a country is credible if allies and adversaries alike will believe it the next time. But as suggested by <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/oxfordhb/9780197541302.013.11">contemporary debates</a> and usage, credibility, in practice, often means something more than simply keeping up with commitments.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Two people walk past a mural depicting a military ship in conflict." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765054/original/file-20261008-50-lupabb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765054/original/file-20261008-50-lupabb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765054/original/file-20261008-50-lupabb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765054/original/file-20261008-50-lupabb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765054/original/file-20261008-50-lupabb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765054/original/file-20261008-50-lupabb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765054/original/file-20261008-50-lupabb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">People in downtown Tehran, Iran, walk past a mural depicting a U.S. aircraft carrier under missile attack.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/home/search?query=war%20in%20iran%20u.s.%20carrier&amp;mediaType=photo">AP Photo/Vahid Salemi</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Credibility is not only about whether nations successfully signal resolve, but also whether relevant audiences perceive their commitments as credible. In other words, contemplating a nation’s credibility is <a href="https://library.fes.de/libalt/journals/swetsfulltext/14965922.pdf">about assumptions over the “strategic culture</a>” that undergird it – and this can include everything from a country’s military resources to abstract notions about its values.</p>

<p>Historical examples are useful here, in particular the Vietnam War, during which American credibility was at stake in unprecedented ways.</p>

<p>On the surface, Vietnam posed little intrinsic value to the United States – it was not a primary theater of the Cold War by most measures. Yet policymakers repeatedly insisted that Vietnam was the place where American credibility had to be demonstrated and established. Why?</p>

<p>Secretary of State John Foster Dulles <a href="https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v12p1/d141">warned in 1954</a> that communist expansion in Asia posed “a grave threat to the whole free community” and insisted that demonstrating resolve would prevent greater dangers later. National security adviser McGeorge Bundy <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-90068-6">similarly argued</a> that the “international prestige of the United States” was deeply invested in Vietnam.</p>

<p>Credibility, to them, meant more than simply honoring commitments. Rather, it was bound up with broader questions of power, honor and <a href="https://www.historynewsnetwork.org/article/the-return-of-the-domino-theory">America’s place in the world</a> between competing powers. </p>

<h2>Prestige, or the lack thereof</h2>

<p>As diplomatic historian Robert McMahon <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/24912130">observed decades ago</a>, credibility has often been treated as if it were a concrete and measurable concept. Yet in practice it has always carried an important symbolic dimension – credibility has come to be a shorthand for American prestige itself.</p>

<p>And that variant of American credibility has in particular rested on anxieties about the continued dominance and superiority of the U.S.-led world order.</p>

<p>During one congressional discussion in 1965, U.S. policymakers warned that withdrawing from Vietnam would mean surrendering “all Asia to Communists,” prompting <a href="https://home.uncg.edu/%7Ejwjones/world/readings/LBJ.pdf">the reflection</a>: “If a nation with 14 million can make Uncle Sam run, what will China think?” </p>

<p>An exchange between President Lyndon Johnson and Undersecretary of State George Ball in 1965 is even more illustrative. President Johnson <a href="https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1964-68v03/d71">worried that abandoning</a> Vietnam would make “all these countries say that Uncle Sam was a paper tiger” and wondered whether America would lose the credibility built by three presidents. Ball’s response was, “No sir. The worst blow would be that the mightiest power on earth is unable to defeat a handful of guerrillas.”</p>

<p>The anxiety was not that America might fail to keep up with its word, but that the leader of the “free world” might fail to defeat a non-Western, technologically inferior opponent.</p>

<p>The credibility at stake was both America’s sense of national self and the perceived superiority of a Western-led world order.</p>

<p>Counterintuitively, while the Vietnam War was fought in the eyes of many policymakers to defend U.S. credibility, its conclusion shattered conventional notions of credibility. It called into question the U.S.’s place in the world in an era historians have termed an “<a href="https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674064362">Age of Fracture</a>,” characterized by economic challenges such as stagflation, oil shocks and rising distrust in politics, government and institutions. </p>

<p>For many observers within and outside the U.S., images of the helicopters lifting off and <a href="https://www.history.com/articles/fall-of-saigon-photo-helicopter-evacuation-rooftop-1975">fleeing from Saigon</a> – and thereby deserting allies and a purportedly essential cause in the process – signaled a moment of American and Western decline. The phenomenon even led to a widely used term – “<a href="https://www.brookings.edu/articles/its-called-the-vietnam-syndrome-and-its-back/">Vietnam Syndrome</a>” – referring to the public’s unwillingness thereafter to commit to large-scale foreign interventions and nation-building exercises.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A helicopter is seen hovering over a building." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765003/original/file-20261008-60-8nrgg9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765003/original/file-20261008-60-8nrgg9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=402&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765003/original/file-20261008-60-8nrgg9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=402&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765003/original/file-20261008-60-8nrgg9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=402&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765003/original/file-20261008-60-8nrgg9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=506&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765003/original/file-20261008-60-8nrgg9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=506&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765003/original/file-20261008-60-8nrgg9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=506&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Credibility up to the present</h2>

<p>That image of U.S. decline and impotence is one that has resonated ever since in foreign policy debates.</p>

<p>The perception of the loss of credibility in Vietnam has <a href="https://www.economist.com/interactive/asia/2025/04/25/with-american-credibility-in-doubt-minds-go-back-to-saigon-in-1975">served as a yardstick</a> for planning, assessing and implementing interventions in other regions. It has been both a way of warning about the dangers of rash interventionism and the consequences of hubris, as well as a rallying cry to avoid repeating past errors. yet maintain credibility through actions in places from the Middle East to Latin America.</p>

<p>The credibility issues central to the U.S. administration’s <a href="https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/07/21/trump-end-iran-war-history/">actions today in Iran</a> – and Ukraine, Venezuela and elsewhere – are thus about the U.S.’s living up to pledges and following through to achieve objectives. As with Vietnam, they also concern clustering around nebulous concepts. of and aims about <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2026/03/01/united-states-strikes-attack-iran-khamenei/">not looking weak militarily</a> or diplomatically.</p>

<p>But the Iran example – and particularly the ongoing episodic <a href="https://unctad.org/publication/strait-hormuz-disruptions-implications-global-trade-and-development">closures of the Strait of Hormuz</a> – is one of the best illustrations today of how merely invoking credibility to act is not the same as having an overall endgame strategy.</p>

<p>While some commentators view this currently as a sign of a lack of resolve, or credibility, if we turn to Iranian actions and to the words of Iran’s acting Defense Minister Majid Ebn-e-Reza we find something else. Namely, Tehran views all threats from the United States as “<a href="https://ae.lapresse.it/world-ae/2026/08/02/iran-defence-minister-we-consider-all-threats-to-be-real-and-credible/">real and credible</a>” and “as a reason to bolster its defense.”</p>

<p>The U.S. and Iran agree on one thing in terms of credibility: America can credibly be relied on to carry out overwhelming violence. </p>

<p>But the problem, as it was in the Vietnam War, is that credibly engaging in war and violence is not a substitute for strategy. Credibility is affected deeply by strategic cultural assessments about superiority and inferiority, and notions about when, where, how and for whom the credibility matters.</p>

<p>Moreover, merely establishing credibility to act cannot necessarily overwhelm a resolute adversary, as has been borne out in Iran. In fact, it can also perpetuate never-ending conflict that <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/07/us/politics/trump-iran-retreat.html">serves to undermine the very prestige and world power</a> that it was supposed to enhance.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/289065/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

The perception of the loss of credibility in Vietnam has served as a yardstick for planning, assessing and implementing interventions in other regions

It has been both a way of warning about the dangers of rash interventionism and the consequences of hubris, as well as a rallying cry to avoid repeating past errors. yet maintain credibility through actions in places from the Middle East to Latin America

The credibility issues central to the U.S. administration’s actions today in Iran – and Ukraine, Venezuela and elsewhere – are thus about the U.S.’s living up to pledges and following through to achieve objectives
As with Vietnam, they also concern clustering around nebulous concepts. of and aims about not looking weak militarily or diplomatically

But the Iran example – and particularly the ongoing episodic closures of the Strait of Hormuz – is one of the best illustrations today of how merely invoking credibility to act is not the same as having an overall endgame strategy

While some commentators view this currently as a sign of a lack of resolve, or credibility, if we turn to Iranian actions and to the words of Iran’s acting Defense Minister Majid Ebn-e-Reza we find something else

Namely, Tehran views all threats from the United States as “ real and credible ” and “as a reason to bolster its defense.” The U.S. and Iran agree on one thing in terms of credibility: America can credibly be relied on to carry out overwhelming violence

    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762942/original/file-20260929-50-7b05pr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C5%2C4240%2C2826&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Who controls a pregnancy is one question surrogacy contracts struggle to answer.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/close-up-belly-of-asian-mother-pregnant-40-weeks-royalty-free-image/1467888087">skaman306/Moment via Getty</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Surrogacy arrangements – agreements for someone to carry a pregnancy for the intended parents – <a href="https://armstronginstitute.org/81-hagar-and-mesopotamian-surrogacy-what-a-new-discovery-says">have existed for millennia</a>, and modern surrogacy contracts for <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1997/01/28/nyregion/noel-keane-58-lawyer-in-surrogate-mother-cases-is-dead.html">half a century</a>. </p>

<p>These contracts typically address parental rights, the <a href="https://www.aaml.org/wp-content/uploads/MAT101_12.pdf">possibility of abortion</a>, medical instructions, health insurance and <a href="https://resolve.org/learn/family-building-options/surrogacy/legal-aspects/">payment of expenses</a>, each side with <a href="https://adoptionart.org/assisted-reproduction/intended-parents/gestational-surrogacy/surrogacy-agreements-contract-terms/">its own legal representation</a>. The contracts are usually honored, resulting in <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fertnstert.2016.03.050">thousands of babies</a> born through surrogacy in the U.S., at a cost that <a href="https://eggdonorandsurrogacy.com/how-much-does-surrogacy-cost/">can top US$200,000</a> when agencies are involved.</p>

<p>In a 2026 case, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/22/us/politics/supreme-court-surrogate-abortion-custody.html">surrogate McKenna West</a> refused the intended parents’ request for an abortion after the fetus was diagnosed with a serious heart condition. The case raises an uncomfortable question: What happens when the surrogate’s bodily autonomy collides with the intended parents’ wishes?</p>

<p>As scholars of <a href="https://www.law.gwu.edu/sonia-m-suter">reproductive justice</a> and <a href="https://www.law.virginia.edu/faculty/profile/nrc8g/2915359">family law</a>, we see this case as an example of how rapidly changing abortion laws, reproductive technology and family law can create conflicts that surrogacy contracts cannot necessarily anticipate.</p>

<h2>The West case</h2>

<p><a href="https://perma.cc/4SPK-8CTZ">West’s contract stated</a> that “there shall be a termination of the pregnancy for a fetal abnormality … if the Intended Parents request” it. <a href="https://nypost.com/2026/08/20/opinion/im-the-surrogate-mother-trying-to-save-a-babys-life-but-the-biological-parents-wanted-an-abortion/">She later wrote</a> that “their lawyer and my own former lawyer sent me letters threatening six-figure penalties if I didn’t comply with their demand to terminate.” </p>

<p>Instead, West moved from Alaska to Texas, where she had family support and believed the baby, when born, could <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/DocketPDF/26/26A325/423610/20260909162543949_2026%2009%2009%20Emergency%20Application.pdf">get needed care</a>. Moreover, she knew that <a href="https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/?tab=1&amp;code=HS&amp;chapter=HS.170A&amp;artSec=">Texas bans abortion</a> in almost all circumstances. Meanwhile, the intended parents, who lived in California, <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/supreme-court-stays-out-of-custody-dispute-california-couple-surrogate-baby-heart-defect/">obtained a court order</a> before the birth stating they would become the legal parents once the baby was born.</p>

<p>Before West gave birth, the <a href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/state/texas/2026/08/12/ken-paxton-baby-gabriel-texas-heart-condition-surrogacy-case/91269721007/">Texas attorney general</a> obtained a <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/supreme-court-stays-out-of-custody-dispute-california-couple-surrogate-baby-heart-defect/">court order requiring lifesaving care</a> for the baby, <a href="https://perma.cc/7VMU-9FWJ">stating that</a> “the intended parents have refused to agree that they will consent to the lifesaving surgery.” West sought custody but was willing to drop her claims if the couple <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/texas/news/dallas-judge-surrogacy-custody-fight-sick-newborn/">agreed to the baby’s treatment</a>.</p>

<p>After the Texas courts upheld the intended parents’ rights, West <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/DocketPDF/26/26A325/423610/20260909162543949_2026%2009%2009%20Emergency%20Application.pdf">asked the Supreme Court to intervene</a> so she could receive “further information about the child she carried for 37 weeks and fought to save.” <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/22/us/politics/supreme-court-surrogate-abortion-custody.html">The court declined</a>, leaving West <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/supreme-court/supreme-court-declines-intervene-custody-case-involving-newborn-heart-rcna597043">no rights to the baby</a>.</p>

<h2>Previous conflicts</h2>

<p>In a similar 2012 case, surrogate Crystal Kelley <a href="https://people.com/parents/surrogate-crystal-kelley-baby-with-birth-defects-parents-order-to-abort/">signed a contract</a> allowing the intended parents to call for an abortion in case of a severe fetal abnormality. When the fetus was diagnosed with a heart defect and other serious anomalies, the parents asked Kelley to terminate the pregnancy. She refused and left Connecticut, where she would not have had parental rights, for Michigan, which at the time would treat her as the legal mother. Kelley placed the baby for adoption, and the girl’s adoptive parents raised her <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2020/08/04/health/seraphina-surrogate-death">until her death at 8</a>. </p>

<p>In the 1988 <a href="https://theconversation.com/becoming-a-parent-through-surrogacy-can-have-ethical-challenges-but-it-is-a-positive-experience-for-some-167760">Baby M case</a>, a surrogate who was also the genetic mother insisted she should be the mother despite signing a contract to relinquish parental rights. The New Jersey Supreme Court <a href="https://law.justia.com/cases/new-jersey/supreme-court/1988/109-n-j-396-1.html">voided that contract</a> because it held that she could not give up her parental rights before birth. As a result, it recognized the surrogate as the legal mother but awarded custody to the father. She <a href="https://www.deseret.com/1988/4/6/18762682/surrogate-mother-granted-expanded-visitation-rights/">later received visitation rights</a>.</p>

<h2>A state-by-state patchwork</h2>

<p>Surrogacy contracts <a href="https://adoptionart.org/assisted-reproduction/intended-parents/gestational-surrogacy/surrogacy-agreements-contract-terms/">establishing legal parentage</a> are enforceable <a href="https://nwsurrogacycenter.com/surrogacy/best-surrogacy-friendly-states-for-intended-parents-and-surrogates/">in a number of states</a>. But <a href="https://connect.asrm.org/lpg/resources/surrogacy-by-state?ssopc=1">surrogacy laws vary</a> by state, <a href="https://petrieflom.law.harvard.edu/2021/02/08/surrogacy-contracts-canceled/">creating a patchwork with respect to enforceability</a>.</p>

<p>West’s journey, for example, involved three states – Alaska, Texas and the intended parents’ state of California. They are <a href="https://nwsurrogacycenter.com/surrogacy/best-surrogacy-friendly-states-for-intended-parents-and-surrogates/">deemed surrogacy-friendly</a>, meaning contracts are relatively easy to enforce there, though the states diverge sharply on abortion.</p>

<p>Surrogacy agreements may <a href="https://adoptionart.org/assisted-reproduction/intended-parents/gestational-surrogacy/surrogacy-agreements-contract-terms/">require the surrogate</a> to restrict travel, eat nutritiously and cooperate with healthcare providers. As in the West and Kelley cases, agreements may also specify when the surrogate could be asked to abort or, if pregnant with multiple fetuses, selectively terminate.</p>

<p>These abortion provisions have rarely been tested in court, and West’s case hasn’t resolved whether they are enforceable. Rather, they raise the question: Can anyone be forced to have an abortion?</p>

<p>After the Supreme Court’s <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/21pdf/19-1392_6j37.pdf">2022 Dobbs decision</a>, which held there is no fundamental right to abortion, states have determined their own abortion laws. In states like Texas, abortion provisions in surrogacy contracts are unenforceable. But even where abortion is legal, a court would likely refuse to <a href="https://www.aaml.org/wp-content/uploads/MAT101_12.pdf">compel an abortion</a>, given the surrogate’s bodily autonomy. </p>

<p>A surrogate’s control over her body may be more limited, however, when intended parents seek to enforce provisions meant to protect the fetus. </p>

<p>If a physician recommends a C-section for the fetus’s well-being and the surrogate refuses, for example, a court might <a href="https://adoptionart.org/assisted-reproduction/intended-parents/gestational-surrogacy/surrogacy-agreements-contract-terms/">enforce a contract clause</a> requiring her “to cooperate with her medical providers.” </p>

<p>Even <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/21pdf/19-1392_6j37.pdf">before 2022</a>, when abortion was still a federal constitutional right, <a href="https://www.propublica.org/article/florida-court-ordered-c-sections">courts in some</a> – <a href="https://www.plainsite.org/opinions/ojhkshh1/in-re-baby-boy-doe/">but not all</a> – jurisdictions ordered C-sections against the pregnant person’s wishes. </p>

<p>In other words, bodily autonomy has never been absolute for pregnant people.</p>

<h2>A post-Dobbs world</h2>

<p>Since Dobbs, surrogacy and abortion have become increasingly intertwined.</p>

<p>In 2025, a Florida judge questioned <a href="https://floridalawweekly.com/00sup67714/sup33_8.pdf">the constitutionality of surrogacy</a> on fetal-personhood grounds – the legal theory that an unborn fetus or embryo has the same legal rights as a born human – even as he granted the intended parents parental rights. </p>

<p><a href="https://floridalawweekly.com/00sup67714/sup33_8.pdf">In his view</a>, there can be no “contractual ownership interest over the unborn baby.” Florida’s attorney general took the argument further, declaring that the couple’s contract with the surrogate violated the 13th Amendment’s <a href="https://www.miamiherald.com/news/politics-government/state-politics/article315673958.html">ban on slavery</a>. <a href="https://www.livenowfox.com/news/surrogacy-is-modern-day-slavery-florida-ag-argues-he-aims-stop-practice">A spokesperson said he was concerned</a> “about any case where a surrogacy company profits off the sale of children.” </p>

<p>Some conservative legislators and advocacy groups have also been challenging the legitimacy of surrogacy, a few with plans <a href="https://19thnews.org/2026/08/surrogacy-restrictions-texas-abortion-opponents/">to limit or even ban it</a>. Consequently, in states that take fetal and embryo personhood seriously, <a href="https://www.peifferwolf.com/mckenna-west-makes-texas-a-flashpoint-in-surrogacy-ivf-dispute/">surrogacy contracts</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.q581">even IVF</a> could become unavailable.</p>

<p>West’s case has surfaced starkly different views of what is at stake. For some, surrogacy is a form of baby selling that should not be allowed. For others, it is a way for intended parents to create families and for surrogates to support them.</p>

<p>Surrogacy asks the law to recognize both the interests of people who intend to become parents and the autonomy of the person who is pregnant. Dobbs has made that balance harder to maintain by inviting fetal-personhood principles into areas of law that had not previously treated fetuses or embryos as persons.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291832/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>The oil market that sets today’s gas prices was invented in western Pennsylvania</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764263/original/file-20261006-50-rjxzzw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C93%2C2048%2C1365&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The Oil City Oil Exchange set the price of crude oil for the nation during the late 19th century.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://oilregionlibraries.org/the-oil-exchange-national-transit/">Oil Region Library Association</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The fall of 2026 is a moment of energy centrality, when geopolitics unfolding far away shows up in Americans’ everyday lives. </p>

<p>In Pennsylvania, the <a href="https://gasprices.aaa.com/?state=PA">statewide diesel price averages US$6.50</a> per gallon. In Iowa, farmers are <a href="https://www.radioiowa.com/2026/09/18/iowans-balk-at-gas-price-bounce-and-diesel-is-more-expensive-than-ever-before/">paying more than $6 a gallon</a> for diesel. And in Alaska, unleaded gas <a href="https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/06/03/youd-be-crying-at-the-pump-this-alaska-villages-gas-was-8-44-before-the-iran-war/">runs more than $9 a gallon</a>. </p>

<p>As a distinguished professor of history and environmental studies <a href="https://altoona.psu.edu/person/brian-c-black-phd">at Penn State Altoona</a>, I write widely about <a href="https://www.press.jhu.edu/books/title/2130/petrolia?srsltid=AU7gw4XELu-SpZdWwWg1LASNz0eTukgAzEYwb4SZhpVLUxJ5t6gQF_rz">oil</a> and <a href="https://www.taylorfrancis.com/books/mono/10.4324/9781003414919/energy-north-american-environmental-history-brian-black">energy issues</a>. This moment has me thinking about how the oil industry <a href="https://nwpaheritage.org/tours/show/5">began nearly 170 years ago</a> in northwestern Pennsylvania. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">

<h2>Setting crude prices in Oil City</h2>

<p>In 1859, <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dcnr/recreation/where-to-go/state-parks/find-a-park/oil-creek-state-park/history">Edwin Drake struck oil</a> along Oil Creek near Titusville, Pennsylvania. His well was funded by investors from New Bedford, Massachusetts, who were looking for a replacement for whale oil, which was expensive and challenging to acquire.</p>

<p>The first oil deals were struck on the streets of Oil City, about 90 miles north of Pittsburgh, while traders were still working out basic questions about “rock oil,” as crude was then called: What was it good for, and how much should it cost?</p>

<p>To create a more formal system, the oil traders developed a railroad car <a href="https://oilregionlibraries.org/the-oil-exchange-national-transit/">designed to be a rolling oil exchange</a> on the Oil Creek Railway. It made 13 stops daily between Titusville and Oil City, and trading was conducted on the honor system, with no written certificates of purchase or sale.</p>

<p>As the <a href="https://oilregionlibraries.org/the-oil-exchange-national-transit/">industry quickly grew</a>, an oil exchange office was set up in <a href="https://www.thederrick.com/news/community_news/out-of-the-archives---old-arlington-hotel-in-oc/article_56c80ea3-7873-5b1e-ac2a-cd6fa59fcd63.html">the Arlington Hotel</a> in Oil City. </p>

<p>Traders pushed for a building of their own, arguing that a growing industry needed a more formal market. By 1874, Pennsylvania’s Oil Valley was producing <a href="https://archive.org/download/historyofstandar00tarbuoft/historyofstandar00tarbuoft.pdf">roughly 30,000 barrels of crude oil</a> a day, which sold for an average of about $1.15 a barrel.</p>

<p>Rather than physically moving barrels around, trading had moved from handshakes to paper. Pipelines issued certificates representing the oil in their lines. <a href="https://aoghs.org/oil-almanac/end-of-oil-exchanges/">Traders bought and sold the paper certificates</a> representing oil, often trading the same barrels many times in a single day. As a result, the volume of oil changing hands could reach 10 million to 14 million barrels a day, hundreds of times more than the wells actually produced.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Businessmen are seen outside an ornate building in a black-and-white photo." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764395/original/file-20261006-51-ag5mio.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764395/original/file-20261006-51-ag5mio.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=493&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764395/original/file-20261006-51-ag5mio.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=493&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764395/original/file-20261006-51-ag5mio.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=493&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764395/original/file-20261006-51-ag5mio.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=619&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764395/original/file-20261006-51-ag5mio.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=619&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764395/original/file-20261006-51-ag5mio.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=619&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In April 1874, a group of Oil City oil men <a href="https://100seneca.com/timeline/">received a state charter</a> to form the Oil City Oil Exchange. Construction started in July 1877 at the corner of Center and Seneca streets. </p>

<p>When the Oil Exchange opened in April 1878, <a href="https://oilregionlibraries.org/the-oil-exchange-national-transit/">the local newspaper called it</a> “the largest and most elaborate structure ever erected in the Oil Region.” The building, the paper said, reflected how big the speculative side of the oil trade had become. Standard Oil, <a href="https://guides.loc.gov/this-month-in-business-history/january/standard-oil-established">the nation’s largest oil company at the time</a>, owned by John D. Rockefeller, kept offices in the building.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://aoghs.org/oil-almanac/end-of-oil-exchanges/">Oil City Oil Exchange</a> heavily influenced early crude oil pricing. Brokers there collected 10 cents a barrel from buyers and 5 cents from sellers. </p>

<p>While the Oil City Oil Exchange was the center of the oil industry for nearly two decades, by 1895 Standard Oil had effectively cornered the market. Its chief buyer, Titusville resident Joseph Seep, began paying producers cash directly, at a price Standard set itself. That control lasted until 1911, when the U.S. Supreme Court <a href="https://guides.loc.gov/chronicling-america-standard-oil-monopoly">ruled in a landmark antitrust case</a> that the trust had to be broken into 34 separate companies. </p>

<p>After that, no single company controlled the price of crude oil.</p>

<h2>Who sets the price of oil now</h2>

<p>Predicting oil prices became a much bigger concern after the <a href="https://theconversation.com/this-is-how-the-1970s-oil-shock-played-out-there-are-lessons-for-the-economy-today-278876">oil crises of the 1970s</a>, when sudden price hikes rattled economies around the world.</p>

<p>Today, the price of crude oil is set largely <a href="https://www.api.org/news-policy-and-issues/news/2026/08/19/who-sets-the-price-of-oil">by traders on two exchanges</a>: the New York Mercantile Exchange and the Intercontinental Exchange. Prices there shift from second to second, and gas prices at the pump follow them, usually within days or weeks.</p>

<p>Much of that trading involves futures contracts, which are agreements to buy oil at a set price on a future date. In the U.S., the benchmark contract is for oil delivered to Cushing, Oklahoma, a storage hub where many of the country’s pipelines meet.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764397/original/file-20261006-51-g1i0uc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A Shell gas station sign lists gas prices." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764397/original/file-20261006-51-g1i0uc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764397/original/file-20261006-51-g1i0uc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764397/original/file-20261006-51-g1i0uc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764397/original/file-20261006-51-g1i0uc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764397/original/file-20261006-51-g1i0uc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764397/original/file-20261006-51-g1i0uc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764397/original/file-20261006-51-g1i0uc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/gas-prices-are-displayed-at-a-gas-station-in-new-york-the-news-photo/2295004534?phrase=New%20York%20Mercantile%20Exchange&amp;adppopup=true">Xinhua News Agency via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The latest shock to that system began this year. War began on Feb. 28, 2026, when the U.S. and Israel launched <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Strait_of_Hormuz_campaign">airstrikes on Iranian military targets</a> that killed Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Iran struck back with missiles and drones and began <a href="https://www.globalsecurity.org/military/ops/iran-war-20260302.htm">attacking commercial ships</a> in the waters around the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula that connects the Persian Gulf to the open ocean. </p>

<p>Within days, the attacks and a wave of canceled shipping insurance brought tanker traffic nearly to a halt. </p>

<p>On March 2, a Revolutionary Guard commander made the closure official in a statement <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/iran-vows-attack-any-ship-trying-pass-through-strait-hormuz-2026-03-02/">carried by Iran’s state media</a>: “The Strait of Hormuz is closed. If anyone tries to pass, the heroes of the Revolutionary Guards and the regular navy will set those ships ablaze.” </p>

<p><a href="https://app.al-monitor.com/originals/2026/06/us-renews-iran-attacks-tehran-says-it-closed-strait-hormuz">Roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil</a> normally passes through the strait. Most of it goes to Asia, not the U.S. But because oil is traded on a global market, <a href="https://theconversation.com/oil-and-gas-industry-expected-surplus-but-war-brought-shortage-instead-292406">prices rose everywhere</a>.</p>

<p>Oil and gas prices kept climbing as peace talks failed. By May 2026, the average price of a gallon of regular gas in the U.S. was 50% higher than before the war began. Since then, Gulf oil producers have <a href="https://abcnews.com/US/wireStory/gulf-nations-found-ways-oil-flowing-iran-war-136708375">found ways around the blockade</a>, sending oil through pipelines to ports outside the strait and through a U.S.-guarded shipping route near Oman. By late September, those work-arounds had restored about half of the oil that normally passes through the strait, helping keep crude prices around $100 a barrel instead of the much higher levels many analysts had feared.</p>

<p>Oil City’s exchange building is long gone. It was torn down in 1926 to make way for a bank. But the market its traders built, where paper claims on oil change hands far faster than the oil itself moves, still sets what drivers pay at the pump in Oil City and everywhere else.</p>

title: The Trump administration plans a public killing

body: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks from a stage in Sparrows Point, Maryland, on October 6, 2026. | Win McNamee/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: The Trump administration is planning a public killing.  What’s happening? On Thursday, the Pentagon announced that it would execute Nidal Hasan, a former Army major sentenced to death for a 2009 mass shooting on a military base, publicly and on livestream.  The execution, if it happens, would be unprecedented: The last widely reported public execution in the US was 90 years ago , in Kentucky, but to stream a death live would be something else entirely

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has promoted the announcement with something approaching glee, telling a reporter that “we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it.” What’s the context? According to the Pentagon, Hasan will be executed via firing squad on December 3 — the first such execution by the military in more than 80 years

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, was sentenced to death in 2013 by a military jury following a court-martial for the 2009 shooting, when he killed 13 people and wounded more than 30 at Fort Hood in Texas
The execution is set to be carried out at the same Army post
Will the Pentagon go through with this? It’s unclear, for multiple reasons

The Pentagon’s announcement that Hasan’s death will be livestreamed has generated a great deal of bipartisan pushback, as well as condemnation by religious groups , though that is unlikely to stop the execution itself.  The head of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops decried the decision to livestream the execution as “a barbaric promotion of a culture of death,” and retiring Sen

Thom Tillis (R-NC) called it the decision “beyond disgusting.”  “Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do,” Tillis wrote in a post on X.  On Friday, Vice President JD Vance also said that he was unsure if the livestream would take place .  Hasan’s legal team could also delay the execution substantially — potentially for multiple years — by challenging his detention in federal court, though he has exhausted the military appeals process
And with that, it’s time to log off… The driest (non-polar) desert in the world, the Atacama in South America, was in full bloom late last month after record-setting rainfall

title: America’s good hurricane luck is about to run out
excerpt: People look out at the waves churning in the ocean as Hurricane Isaias approaches. | Joe Raedle/Getty Images This story appeared in  Today, Explained, &nbs
body: People look out at the waves churning in the ocean as Hurricane Isaias approaches. | Joe Raedle/Getty Images This story appeared in  Today, Explained,  a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here
The first hurricane of the fall season is expected to strike the Gulf Coast overnight, marking the latest onset of hurricane season in living memory
As of early Friday afternoon, Hurricane Isaias had grown to a Category 3 storm, with sustained winds of 120 miles per hour
It will strike along the shores of the Florida Panhandle, Alabama, and Mississippi, posing a threat to life and property for millions of Americans
Weather forecasters anticipate between 8 and 12 inches of rain in the areas near where the storm makes landfall
Isaias’s imminent arrival signals the end of a period of unusual good luck when it comes to hurricanes striking the United States
Last year, no hurricanes reached the US mainland at all
And this year, Isaias is breaking a more than 100-year-old record: October 9 is the latest date since 1905 for the first Atlantic hurricane of the season to take shape
August and September have historically been the busiest periods of hurricane season
It’s a strange recent phenomenon, and it’s been even more fortuitous than it would ordinarily be

That’s because the Trump administration has slashed weather forecasting and emergency relief funding over the past two years, leaving us less prepared for a disaster.  And now our luck seems to be running out — with even more rough weather on the way

Hurricane season may be quieter than usual — but El Niño is on the way Here’s the secret ingredient that’s pushed off hurricanes even as warming planetary temperatures raise concerns about more extreme weather events: El Niño

This notorious shift in global wind patterns, which occurs every two to seven years, moves warm water around the oceans, disrupting traditional weather patterns and leading to intense rain and sometimes disastrous flooding, as well as droughts
If there is an upside, however, it’s that this temporary change in ocean conditions prevents hurricanes from forming as frequently as they otherwise would
The downside is, well, El Niño is still on its way
Forecasters expect this year’s version to be historically bad — using words like “super” or “Godzilla” to describe it

The worst of the bad weather is projected to arrive in December: The southern half of the continental US is expected to see unusually rainy and stormy weather, while areas of the Great Lakes and Pacific Northwest could see extreme dry spells.  It will also serve as a crucial test of our reduced capacity for predicting and responding to disasters

Trump’s “big beautiful bill” cut funding for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s weather forecasting and public alert programs by $200 million, and 17 percent of FEMA’s workforce left the agency in 2025 amid the administration’s DOGE purge.  For now, if you’re in the danger zone for Isaias, please pay attention to local and national weather alerts this weekend
If you’re not, count yourself lucky — but there are storm clouds on the horizon
