title: Who are the violent Israeli settlers in the West Bank?
excerpt: A destroyed car sits outside a burnt home in the West Bank village of Jalud on September 29, 2026. | Erik Marmor/Getty Images In the weeks and months following
body: A destroyed car sits outside a burnt home in the West Bank village of Jalud on September 29, 2026. | Erik Marmor/Getty Images In the weeks and months following Hamas’s brutal October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, and Israel’s devastating campaign in Gaza that followed, the world’s attention turned away from the West Bank.  Over the past three years, however, the situation in the Israel-occupied territory has worsened as Israeli settlers have carried out more violent attacks on Palestinians

The attacks can range from acts of daily harassment and trespassing to a major mob assault in the West Bank village of Jalud that overwhelmed Israeli security forces and blocked a displaced Palestinian family from returning home
Last week, Israeli settlers shot and killed a Palestinian man

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has largely dismissed violent West Bank settlers as an issue, blaming the Jalud attack on a “handful of rioters” and referring to settlers as “juvenile delinquents” in a speech to the UN last month , in which he argued that the world should focus on violence committed by Palestinians instead
But even as he downplays the problem, human rights organizations have documented a record level of Israeli settler violence in the West Bank
The International Committee of the Red Cross has said that such attacks have made everyday life “untenable” for the more than 3 million Palestinians living in the West Bank
The Israeli settlements are also clearly illegal, as Vox’s Zack Beauchamp explained in September — but that hasn’t stopped them from expanding

Ahead of Israel’s elections later this month, settlers have accelerated a campaign of ethnic cleansing with the explicit backing of some Israeli cabinet ministers , led by young militant Jewish settlers that are part of a loose network known as the Hilltop Youth
The Wall Street Journal’s Feliz Solomon reported on the Jalud attack and has written about the role of Hilltop Youth in worsening settler violence
She spoke with Today, Explained co-host Noel King about the reality on the ground in the West Bank, the settler groups behind it, and how Israeli officials are responding
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
Tell me about the last three years in the West Bank

What’s been happening? The October 7 attack really hardened a lot of people’s views in Israel, and that’s played out in the West Bank in a number of ways.  One is that the government of Benjamin Netanyahu, which has some powerful members who are settlers themselves, became much more overtly supportive of expanding the Jewish settlements.  The second thing that changed was basically a total breakdown of trust, both between Jews and Arabs, and also between Jews and the state, because a lot of people felt that they were really on their own in terms of security.  All of this created a really combustible environment
They’re behaving more brazenly, and there’s what a lot of people would describe as a permissive environment of almost total impunity
What does that total impunity look like? We often hear the term “settler violence.” What does that mean? There’s really a whole spectrum of violent actions
It’s mostly by younger male settlers
There are some acts of daily harassment, like trespassing on Palestinian property, vandalism, stalking people, blocking roads, and preventing access to resources like water wells
And then on the other end of the spectrum, there are also acts of extreme violence.  There have been some very serious physical assaults
Last year, there was a viral video of an elderly woman who was beaten with a stick
And lately, we’ve been seeing more mob violence where a large group of settlers will raid a Palestinian village

They’ve set mosques and other property on fire.  Just to be clear, there’s violence by Palestinians too, but we’re really seeing an alarming surge of violence by settlers that’s often unpunished, and increasingly it’s happening when settlers go into Palestinian areas where they’re not supposed to be
You reported on an attack that happened last week in the West Bank near the Palestinian village of Jalud

Over the summer, some young settlers who are associated with a group called the Hilltop Youth set up an encampment around three houses on the outskirts of the Palestinian village, Jalud, and essentially besieged the houses
They blocked their access to essential goods and harassed the residents until, in late July, they felt so unsafe that they fled
Two of those houses belonged to the Tubasi family
In early September, Israel’s high court ordered the state to ensure their safe return, and in late September, they tried to go back

We spoke with Wael, who’s one member of the family, and also with their lawyer about what happened when they tried to go back.  A few dozen [Israeli] security forces were deployed to escort them home in the middle of the night, and when they got there, they found that the house was totally ransacked
They showed us before and after pictures, and the windows were smashed, the doors were broken, electrical wires were cut, and there was just debris all over the place

When they came inside for the first time in about two months, they were walking through the property looking at the damage with flashlights, and they’d only been there for a few minutes when suddenly they were surrounded by a mob of settlers

They said at first that there were about 50 settlers around the house, and the military later said that there were more than a hundred people that took part in what they called a riot.  The authorities told the family to take cover deeper inside the house, and they hid inside a stairwell as the soldiers tried to force these settlers to retreat, but they were shouting and throwing rocks at the house, and then, according to Wael, they even started climbing in through the windows
At that point, the authorities told the family to go upstairs, all the way up to the roof and to hide in a corner of the rooftop.  Wael explained what he saw up there
He was looking down and he saw the soldiers battling it out with this large group of settlers and this thick cloud of tear gas and loud bangs from stun grenades. “There are more settlers there now

They’re behaving more brazenly, and there’s what a lot of people would describe as a permissive environment of almost total impunity.” Eventually, the security forces realized that they weren’t getting the situation under control
They took them back downstairs and outside and put them in a military vehicle, but then the settlers surrounded the vehicle and they were rocking the car
They slashed the tires so that [the family] couldn’t leave

Then the soldiers had to move them into an armored military vehicle and eventually they got them out.  A short while later, not long after they had escaped, they started receiving video messages from some of their neighbors that showed what happened after they left, which was that their car and their house had been set on fire
All right, so the Israeli authorities in the form of soldiers were trying to help this Palestinian family legally return and settlers violently blocked them
What do we know about who these settlers are and what is motivating them? This was a very large group
We know of three people who were detained in this incident

title: Antarctica’s penguins are sending us a distress signal
excerpt: Chinstrap and macaroni penguins nesting on the volcanic slopes of Zavodovski Island. | Nicole Richters via British Antarctic Survey This story was originally pu
body: Chinstrap and macaroni penguins nesting on the volcanic slopes of Zavodovski Island. | Nicole Richters via British Antarctic Survey This story was originally published by The Guardian and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration
The world’s largest penguin colony has declined by two-thirds since 2011, most likely because of the climate crisis, a study has revealed

Scientists said the rapid demise of chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski, the northernmost of the South Sandwich Islands in Antarctica , increased the risk of a wider ecosystem collapse. “It is an enormous population crash, equivalent to half a million breeding individuals being lost from that island,” said the leader of the research, professor Norman Ratcliffe, a penguin ecologist at the British Antarctic Survey

The Guardian reported in 2020 that chinstrap penguin populations were decreasing on Low in the South Shetland Islands, prompting concerns among scientists that “something is broken” in the world’s wildest ecosystem

The new study, published on Wednesday in the journal Current Biology , indicates that the speed of collapse may be accelerating so rapidly that the distinctive bird — which gets its name from a black line that runs below the beak from cheek to cheek — may need to be classified as an endangered species
Zavodovski Island had by far the biggest penguin colony in the world, with about 600,000 chinstraps and 90,000 macaroni penguins when the population was measured in 2011
Given the decline between then and 2025, it is likely to have lost that title to Cape Adare in the Ross Sea
Scientists believe the most likely cause is climate disruption
Human-driven heating has pushed up winter temperatures on and around the Antarctic Peninsula to 5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, one of the fastest rises in the world

On 6 June, the Argentinian Esperanza base on the Trinity Peninsula registered a record winter high of 15.4°C, about 20°C above normal for the time of year — a margin that scientists described as “absolutely crazy.” Chinstrap penguins are struggling to adapt because they have special diets and specific ocean temperature preferences
Tracking data shows they prefer to forage in cooler waters to the northwest of the island, where they would expect to find Antarctic krill, which make up the bulk of their diet
But as the waters warm, the krill have moved south into the Weddell Sea
Macaroni penguins, by contrast, are less fussy eaters and their numbers rose 30 percent — though not nearly enough to make up for the loss of chinstraps
Ratcliffe said this was only small comfort because if current trends continued, all penguins would run out of space

He said the loss of chinstrap penguins would have wider repercussions for food webs. “Each ecosystem could be regarded as like a giant Jenga set, and every component that you remove increases the risk of ecosystems collapsing completely.” The scientists ruled out several other possible causes of decline
There was no sign that chinstrap and macaroni penguins were in competition for food
The nearest humans lived thousands of miles away

Although the island is volcanic and had a major eruption in 2016, prompting a “ Penguin Pompeii hypothesis ” of a sudden population fall, this theory was not borne out either by the data, which showed a steady linear decline, or by observations that showed the chinstraps avoided the main “asphyxia plain” area where the ash and lava were deposited.
